Android background execution: Services, BroadcastReceiver, WorkManager, foreground services, and alarmsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to choose an API by latency, durability, user visibility, and clock precision, explain its real guarantees, design repeatable and interruptible work across process death or reboot, and inspect scheduler state rather than merely proving that an API was called. This section deepens execution reliability instead of repeating the base component catalogue.

Senior mental model#

A component is an entry point, not a resource guarantee. Process lifetime, component lifetime, thread lifetime, and durable-job lifetime are distinct. The system may defer a start, stop a component or job, kill the process, or lose alarms at reboot. Correctness comes from a durable source of truth, idempotent effects, checkpoints, and reconciliation—not from hoping that a callback completes.

  • Process ≠ component: the system raises process importance while a component handles a callback or active binding, but the process is not immortal. After the callback, do not rely on a thread, singleton, or process-scoped coroutine.
  • Scheduling ≠ execution time: enqueueing work or setting an alarm records intent. Constraints, Doze, App Standby, quota, battery restriction, thermal state, and OEM policy influence the actual start.
  • Persistence ≠ exactly once: WorkManager stores the request and attempts eligible execution, but a crash between an external side effect and a local commit can cause replay. Design at-least-once-like handling without claiming a formal delivery guarantee: stable operation IDs, idempotency keys, transactional outbox/inbox, upsert, and resumable checkpoints.

Internals: ownership, scheduling, and interruption#

Started and bound Services#

By default, a Service runs callbacks on the main thread of its hosting process; it does not create a background thread or a separate process. Blocking I/O or CPU work in a callback can cause an ANR, so use explicitly managed coroutines or executors with cancellation.

  • Started: startService()/startForegroundService() leads to onStartCommand(intent, flags, startId). The service continues independently of the caller until stopSelf(startId)/stopService() or the system stops it. Repeated starts produce start IDs but share one Service instance. START_NOT_STICKY, START_STICKY, and START_REDELIVER_INTENT are restart policies after a kill, not completion or exactly-once guarantees.
  • Bound: bindService() exposes an IBinder, and lifetime usually follows clients. Local Binder calls can run on the caller thread; remote calls use Binder threads, so thread safety and a non-blocking contract must be explicit. onServiceDisconnected() reports a lost connection after crash/kill, not a normal unbind.
  • A Service may be both started and bound: unbinding does not end the started lifetime, while stopSelf() does not destroy it while bindings remain. A separate android:process adds IPC, a failure boundary, and memory cost, but not durability.

Background-service limits introduced in Android 8 (API 26) constrain background apps: after a grace window, ordinary background services must stop. Prefer WorkManager/JobScheduler for deferrable durable work and a lawful FGS for ongoing user-visible work.

BroadcastReceiver: registration, trust, and time budget#

  • A manifest receiver can start the process for an allowed broadcast. For apps targeting API 26+, most implicit broadcasts cannot be declared in the manifest except documented exceptions. A context receiver exists only while its registering context is valid; register and unregister symmetrically to avoid leaking an Activity.
  • For runtime registration, explicitly choose ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED for app-only broadcasts or RECEIVER_EXPORTED when other apps or all privileged system senders are required. Exported controls reachability, not authorisation: sensitive actions still require permissions, explicit package/component where applicable, and payload validation.
  • onReceive() uses the main thread unless a scheduler is supplied and must finish quickly. goAsync() only extends the broadcast lifetime through a PendingResult; call finish() in finally. Official guidance still expects very quick completion, roughly under 10 seconds. It is not a long-work mechanism. For durable continuation, enqueue WorkManager/JobScheduler and return.

WorkManager: durable intent, policy, and data flow#

WorkManager is the recommended Jetpack scheduler for deferrable, guaranteed-to-be-scheduled persistent work. It stores requests in its internal database so they survive process death and reboot. It is not an exact timer and does not preserve a continuous process. Platform backends vary by API, including JobScheduler on modern Android, and constraints plus system optimisation determine eligible starts.

MechanismSenior-level consequence
ConstraintsNetwork, charging, battery, storage, and idle are conditions for starting and continuing, not a snapshot. If a constraint disappears, the Worker may stop and run later.
Unique workKEEP ignores a new request while an unfinished chain exists; REPLACE cancels existing work; APPEND inherits prerequisite failure/cancellation; APPEND_OR_REPLACE starts a new sequence after a failed/cancelled chain. A unique name deduplicates scheduling, not the external side effect.
Retry/backoffResult.retry() applies linear or exponential inexact backoff. The minimum initial delay is 10 seconds; the default is exponential with 30 seconds. Permanent input/domain errors should not retry forever.
ExpeditedFor short, user-important, latency-sensitive work and subject to system quota. OutOfQuotaPolicy explicitly downgrades to regular work or drops the request. “Expedited” never means immediate under every condition.
Foreground workersetForeground() runs a WorkManager-managed FGS with a notification for long work. FGS rules still apply; from Android 16, long-running workers can consume job quota.
Cancellation/stopCancellation changes state and sends a stop signal. A CoroutineWorker must not swallow cancellation; blocking loops check isStopped. A Result produced after stop is ignored. Close files, DB, and network resources and keep operations resumable.
Data/chainsData is a lightweight primitives/arrays container with serialized MAX_DATA_BYTES = 10,240 for input/output, not a datastore. Pass IDs or URIs; keep payload in a DB/file. Success unblocks dependents; failure/cancellation propagates downstream; an InputMerger needs explicit conflict semantics.

For side effects, persist an operation row before enqueueing, use a logical unique name, and let the Worker claim and read current durable state transactionally. A server idempotency key closes the crash window between HTTP success and local commit; local unique work alone cannot.

Foreground services: visible ongoing work, not an escape hatch#

  • An FGS is for work the user can notice. startForegroundService() creates the service, but the service must promptly call ServiceCompat.startForeground() (the platform deadline is a few seconds, traditionally described as 5 seconds) with an ongoing notification or the system stops the app/service.
  • Apps targeting Android 12 / API 31+ generally cannot start an FGS from the background except documented exemptions; violation throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. While-in-use camera, microphone, location, and body-sensor prerequisites add further restrictions.
  • Declare android:foregroundServiceType, the base FOREGROUND_SERVICE permission, and type-specific permissions/prerequisites. Target API 34+ enforces types and permissions more strictly. The type must match real work; notification-channel or notification-permission UX does not remove the notification obligation.
  • Android 14 (API 34) introduced user-initiated data transfer jobs for long uploads/downloads explicitly started by the user. This is a JobScheduler API, requires an ongoing notification, and needs a fallback on older APIs. Use expedited WorkManager for short transfers and consider DownloadManager where its purpose-built model fits.

AlarmManager, Doze, and civil time#

  • Prefer an inexact alarm: set(), setWindow(), and setInexactRepeating() permit batching and save battery. An alarm opens only a short execution window; its receiver should enqueue durable work instead of running a network loop.
  • Use setExact*/setAlarmClock() only for genuinely user-facing precise time. Android 12 / target 31+ requires exact-alarm special access for SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM. Android 13+ offers the restricted USE_EXACT_ALARM alternative only for qualifying core use cases. Check canScheduleExactAlarms(); revocation cancels future exact alarms.
  • Doze defers ordinary alarms, jobs, and network. setAndAllowWhileIdle()/setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() are throttled and do not grant long network execution; setAlarmClock() is the most disruptive user-alarm option. App Standby, battery restriction, and OEM policy can constrain work further.
  • ELAPSED_REALTIME resists wall-clock/time-zone changes but resets at reboot; RTC follows wall-clock time. All alarms disappear on shutdown: rebuild from a durable domain schedule after BOOT_COMPLETED. For “09:00 local,” store the time zone and civil-time rule, handle time/time-zone changes, and compute the next occurrence rather than adding 24-hour milliseconds.

Guarantee / non-guarantee matrix#

Safe claimDo not promise
Service callbacks normally arrive on the hosting process main thread.A Service automatically creates a thread/process or survives a kill.
goAsync() keeps a broadcast pending until finish() within a short budget.A receiver can reliably finish a long upload after returning.
WorkManager persists the scheduled request and reschedules eligible work.Exact time, exactly-once side effects, unlimited runtime, or execution after force-stop.
An FGS exposes ongoing work and raises process importance.Immortality, bypassing quota/start rules, or unlimited duration.
An exact alarm with access narrows timing tolerance.Arbitrary long work at an exact millisecond under all system/OEM conditions.
Reconciliation and idempotency make replay safe.Every scheduler formally provides at-least-once or exactly-once delivery.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • API 26 / Android 8: background-service limits and manifest implicit-broadcast restrictions; legacy IntentService is not a modern replacement.
  • API 31 / Android 12 target+: background FGS starts are denied by default and exact alarms require special access. Inspect runtime state, not only the manifest.
  • API 33 / Android 13 target+: notification runtime permission affects app-notification visibility, but an FGS must still supply a notification; USE_EXACT_ALARM is restricted to qualifying categories.
  • API 34 / Android 14 target+: required FGS types, type-specific permissions, and runtime prerequisites; UIDT jobs start at API 34. Cached apps can receive some less important broadcasts later.
  • API 35 / Android 15 target+: dataSync and mediaProcessing FGS types share a per-type six-hours-in-a-rolling-24-hours limit and receive onTimeout(); several FGS types cannot start from BOOT_COMPLETED.
  • Android 16: long-running WorkManager workers using an FGS can consume JobScheduler quota; cross-process broadcast priority is no longer guaranteed. Check target-SDK behavior and current documentation, not only SDK_INT.

Decision framework#

RequirementDefaultWhy / caveat
Only while a screen is visibleLifecycle scope; bound service only for shared IPC/resourceDo not turn UI work into a durable job.
Deferrable and survives process/rebootWorkManagerConstraints, unique policy, retry, idempotent Worker; timing is inexact.
Short important user-triggered workExpedited WorkManagerQuota and explicit out-of-quota policy.
Ongoing visible session (media/location/device)Typed FGS or purpose-built APIVisible notification, start eligibility, permission, and stop action.
Long user-initiated upload/downloadUIDT job on API 34+, versioned fallbackUser-visible transfer; JobScheduler rather than a Jetpack wrapper.
Precise user-facing clock eventExact AlarmManager only if necessarySpecial access and reboot/time-zone reconstruction.
Event may be batchedInexact alarm or WorkManagerChoose clock trigger versus durable constrained work.
Short reaction to a system/app eventReceiver → validate → enqueuegoAsync() only for brief completion.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Lower latency costs quota, battery, or user interruption; stronger durability adds database state, retries, deduplication, and migrations.
  • Constraints reduce waste but can starve work. Expose pending/last-synced state, allow manual retry, and reconcile when the app opens.
  • REPLACE can lose progress, KEEP can retain stale inputs, and APPEND can create a long poisoned chain. Make the Worker read current durable state and choose policy from domain semantics.
  • Force-stop, user battery restriction, permission revocation, low storage, reboot, and an OEM task killer are distinct test states. No app API can promise execution when platform or user deliberately blocks the app.
  • Retry without failure taxonomy turns a 401 or validation error into a battery-draining loop; cancellation without cooperative cleanup leaves partial files or locks; an FGS without a stop path is a UX and policy defect.

Production scenario: offline outbox plus user-visible attachment#

Hypothetically: a chat app stores a message and stable operationId in a Room outbox transaction, then enqueues unique WorkManager sync. Under a network constraint, the Worker claims pending rows, sends a server idempotency key, atomically records the acknowledgement, and retries only transient failure. Process death anywhere leads to reconciliation rather than a duplicate message.

A small message uses an expedited request with downgrade policy. A large attachment explicitly started by the user uses a UIDT job on API 34+, with progress notification and a documented versioned fallback. User cancel marks the domain operation cancelled, cancels the scheduler handle, and cooperative abort deletes the partial temporary file. After reboot the outbox remains the source of truth; UI reports pending or failed rather than inventing delivery.

Code-review/debugging trap#

override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
    GlobalScope.launch { api.upload(intent.getStringExtra("path")!!) }
}

class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        api.upload(inputData.getString("path")!!) // no idempotency/checkpoint
        return Result.success()
    }
}

The receiver process can die immediately after return; a raw path is untrusted or stale, GlobalScope is not durable, the Worker can replay after remote success, and cancellation may be swallowed. Ask where the durable operation row lives, how sender/URI is validated, which unique policy applies, how transient and permanent errors differ, where the server idempotency key and checkpoint live, what cleanup and user visibility exist, and how stop/reboot/quota is reproduced. Fix with a short receiver → transaction/outbox → ID-based WorkManager pipeline, cooperative cancellation, and reconciliation.

Testing and debugging#

adb shell dumpsys activity services com.example.app
adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler
adb shell dumpsys alarm
adb shell am force-stop com.example.app
adb shell am kill com.example.app
adb shell cmd jobscheduler run -f com.example.app JOB_ID
adb shell cmd jobscheduler get-job-state com.example.app JOB_ID
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle
adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.example.app rare
# Android 15 device: exercise the FGS timeout path
adb shell am compat enable FGS_INTRODUCE_TIME_LIMITS com.example.app

Use WorkManager's work-testing: TestWorkerBuilder for Worker logic and WorkManagerTestInitHelper/TestDriver for delays, periods, and constraints. On devices, assert database transitions, idempotency keys, retry classification, duplicate enqueue, constraint loss during a run, cancellation cleanup, process kill, reboot/reschedule, denied exact-alarm access, Doze/standby, and notification stop actions—not merely “the callback happened.” Restore device state after manual power tests.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why is a Service not a background thread? It is a component and lifecycle entry point; callbacks normally use the hosting process main thread. Threading and cancellation are separate design choices.
  2. Started versus bound Service? A started Service follows explicit stop policy independently of the caller; a bound Service serves clients. Both lifetimes may coexist and both must end before destruction.
  3. When should a receiver use goAsync()? For brief asynchronous completion within roughly a ten-second budget and with finish() guaranteed. Enqueue long durable work.
  4. What does WorkManager guarantee? Persistent scheduling and execution when constraints and the system permit—not exact timing or an exactly-once external effect.
  5. Why unique work if the Worker is idempotent? Unique work controls scheduler duplication and chain policy; idempotency separately protects domain effects and crash windows. Both layers matter.
  6. Retry or failure? Retry transient conditions with backoff; fail permanent input/domain errors. Authentication can require refresh or user action rather than infinite retry.
  7. Expedited work versus FGS? Expedited work is short, latency-sensitive queued work under quota; an FGS is ongoing user-visible work with notification, type, permissions, and start restrictions.
  8. When is an exact alarm justified? Only when a core user-facing function needs precise time. Otherwise an inexact alarm or WorkManager gives batching and better battery behavior.
  9. What survives reboot? A WorkManager request and your durable database state; AlarmManager alarms do not and must be reconstructed. An in-memory service or coroutine does not survive.
  10. How do you prevent duplicate execution? Stable operation identity, transactional state transitions, a server idempotency key or upsert, checkpoints, and reconciliation—without calling the scheduler formally exactly once.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. HTTP 200 arrived, then the process died before the DB commit. The next run can repeat the call; a server idempotency key returns the same result and the Worker reconciles the acknowledgement atomically.
  2. A network constraint disappears during upload. WorkManager's stop signal does not roll back the network. Abort cooperatively, store a resumable offset/session, close resources, and safely continue or restart.
  3. “Every day at 09:00” fires at 08:00 after DST. The implementation stored an elapsed or 24-hour interval rather than a civil-time rule. Store zone plus local time and recompute the next instant after each fire, time-zone change, and reboot.
  4. A foreground Worker on Android 16 stops starting under load. Long-running workers can exhaust job quota. Inspect stop reason and quota; use UIDT for a user-started transfer, a lawful typed FGS for a direct ongoing case, or chunk/defer the work.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Which durable record and idempotency key protect your most important background side effect?
  2. What happens if the process dies before start, during I/O, and after remote success?
  3. Which API fits the latency, durability, visibility, and clock precision of your case?
  4. How does your code react to constraint loss, cancellation, force-stop, reboot, and a time-zone change?
  5. Which dumpsys or test-driver assertions prove a state transition rather than merely a callback?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you choose and design reliable background execution on Android?

~30-second answer#

I separate process, component, and durable-work lifetimes. For deferrable work that must survive process death or reboot I default to WorkManager with constraints, unique-work policy, bounded retries, and idempotent effects. A service is not a thread; a foreground service is only for ongoing user-visible work and must satisfy start, type, permission, and notification rules. Broadcast receivers stay short and enqueue durable work. Alarms are for clock events, exact only when the user-facing requirement justifies special access. I test cancellation, duplicates, Doze, process death, and reboot.

~2-minute answer#

I begin with four requirements: latency, durability across process death or reboot, user visibility, and clock precision. UI-scoped work remains lifecycle-scoped. Deferrable persistent work goes to WorkManager; short important work may be expedited, but quota and out-of-quota behavior are explicit. Ongoing user-visible work may require a correctly typed foreground service or a purpose-built API such as a user-initiated data-transfer job.

A Service is an Android component, not a background thread. Its callbacks normally run on the process main thread. Started and bound lifetimes are independent, and neither makes the process immortal. A receiver is also a short entry point: goAsync extends the broadcast only briefly, so durable continuation is persisted and enqueued.

For WorkManager I model constraints, unique-work conflict policy, transient versus permanent failure, backoff, cooperative stop, and chain failure propagation. Data carries small IDs, not payloads. Persistence still does not make an external side effect exactly once: a crash after server success but before local commit can replay it. I use an operation ID, transactional outbox, server idempotency key, checkpoints, and reconciliation.

AlarmManager is for clock-driven delivery. I prefer inexact alarms, reserve exact alarms for justified user-facing precision, check special access, and rebuild schedules after reboot or civil-time changes. Finally, I verify DB transitions and stop reasons with WorkManager test drivers, adb and dumpsys under constraint loss, quota, Doze, cancellation, process death, reboot, and OEM-restricted conditions.

Android permissions, storage, and notifications across versionsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to design capability flows that remain correct after denial, process recreation, Settings changes, OS or target SDK upgrades, and narrowed access; select the least-privileged storage and notification API; distinguish Android platform behavior from Google Play, OEM, and app policy; and reproduce critical states with tests and adb.

Senior mental model#

A permission is not a dialog or Boolean; it is a revocable capability. Effective access depends on device API, targetSdk, manifest declarations, current grant/app-op/channel state, lifecycle, and the resource. A request merely starts a system-mediated transition. Re-check immediately before every sensitive operation and provide a degraded path.

  • Platform behavior: runtime grants, one-time and while-in-use scope, auto-reset, scoped storage, channel state, and package visibility are Android/API contracts.
  • Distribution policy: Google Play eligibility for background location, all-files access, or full-screen intents is a separate review and policy layer. A manifest declaration or device grant does not prove policy compliance.
  • OEM/app policy: a manufacturer can add settings, battery/privacy UX, or defects, while the product can add a pre-prompt. Do not present any OEM behavior as universal Android behavior; record the tested device and firmware.
  • Minimize first: Photo Picker, SAF, system pickers, Companion Device Manager, and app-specific storage often remove broad permissions. Collect only required data for the minimum retention period with explicit deletion semantics.

Internals and state transitions#

Permission state machine and UX#

Observable stateActionCaveat
GrantedRun the feature after checking scope: foreground/background, coarse/fine, or selected media.The grant can change outside the app through Settings, auto-reset, policy, upgrade, or one-time expiry.
Not requestedThe app records its own request history, explains context, and asks at the moment of value.The platform has no universal separate “never asked” enum.
Denied + rationaleExplain the need without coercion; allow retry or degraded mode.shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() is a UX hint, not a complete state machine.
Denied without rationale after a requestAvoid request loops; explain the feature and open app Settings only after explicit user action.shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() is not a complete permanent-denial oracle: false can mean before the first request, “don’t ask again” or repeated denial, policy, or another platform state. Correlate app-owned request history, but trust the current grant.
Partial or temporaryModel coarse, selected photos, while-in-use, and one-time as distinct capabilities.Never display them as full access.

On Android 11+, location, camera, and microphone may be one-time; the system later revokes access and can terminate the process. Auto-reset or app hibernation can reset runtime grants for unused apps. Android 12+ lets the user choose approximate location even when fine is requested: request coarse and fine together, support coarse, and explain precision only where essential. While-in-use does not imply arbitrary background access.

A permission group is presentation and management metadata, not an atomic grant. Request and check each permission; groups and system UI can change across releases. A RequestMultiplePermissions result can be mixed.

Activity Result API, lifecycle, and recreation#

class ImportFragment : Fragment() {
    // Register unconditionally on every creation, in stable order.
    private val requestLocation = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestMultiplePermissions()
    ) { grants ->
        renderLocationAccess(
            coarse = grants[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION] == true,
            fine = grants[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION] == true
        )
    }

    private val pickImage = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia()
    ) { uri -> uri?.let(viewModel::onImageSelected) }
}

ActivityResultRegistry can deliver a pending result after configuration change or process recreation when launchers register unconditionally on every creation and in the same order; launch only when lifecycle state permits. The callback must not depend on an old View or an in-memory “current request.” Store business intent or operation ID in SavedStateHandle or a database, then re-check the permission or URI and current state. Do not relaunch automatically on every recreation.

Location: foreground, precision, and background sequence#

  • Begin foreground flow with ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION; add ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION only when the feature cannot work approximately. On Android 12+, request coarse and fine together; the user can retain approximate only.
  • ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION arrived in Android 10. On Android 11+, obtain foreground access first, then separately educate and route the user through the system Settings flow; a simultaneous foreground-plus-background request does not produce the expected dialog.
  • Background location must support core, user-visible functionality. Android platform restrictions and Google Play background-location policy are separate gates. An FGS location type and while-in-use rules do not replace the background permission.
  • If the user downgrades precise to approximate or revokes location in Settings, Android can restart or kill the app process. Rebuild from durable state and re-check.

Bluetooth, Nearby, media, camera, and microphone#

  • Android 12 / target 31+: BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, and BLUETOOTH_ADVERTISE replace broad legacy Bluetooth and location coupling for corresponding actions. Cap legacy declarations with maxSdkVersion="30". Declare neverForLocation only when scan results truly are not used to derive location because the system may filter some BLE beacons.
  • Android 13 / target 33+: common Wi‑Fi discovery and control uses NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES; media reads split into READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, and READ_MEDIA_AUDIO instead of READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
  • Android 14 / target 34+: READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED represents user-selected photos and videos. If the app does not own a reselection flow, system compatibility mode can manage selection; re-check access on resume and use.
  • Camera and microphone: runtime plus one-time or while-in-use semantics, privacy indicators, and device-wide sensor toggles are separate failure states. A grant does not guarantee hardware availability, exclusive access, sensor privacy state, or a legal background start.

Notifications: permission, channels, and interruption#

  • Android 13 / API 33: non-exempt notifications need runtime POST_NOTIFICATIONS. With target 33+, the app controls contextual timing; target ≤32 has system-controlled timing and tighter re-prompt behavior. Fresh installs begin blocked. Eligible OS upgrades can be pre-granted, while an earlier user block persists.
  • An FGS may start without a POST_NOTIFICATIONS grant, but its notification remains mandatory. After denial, the FGS notice can appear in Task Manager rather than the notification drawer. Use areNotificationsEnabled() and channel state for UX, never to bypass service rules.
  • Channels (API 26+) must exist before posting. Their ID is a long-lived product contract: channels persist, and an app cannot raise importance that the user lowered. After creation the app cannot change importance or sound semantics, though it can update name and description. Never delete and recreate a channel to reset user choice; use a new ID only for genuinely new semantics.
  • App permission, channel importance and user settings, DND, plus system ranking and delivery are separate gates. Importance does not guarantee heads-up; the user and system have final control.
  • Android 12 / target 31+: notification-trampoline restrictions prevent a Service or BroadcastReceiver intermediary from starting an Activity after a tap. Give the notification a direct activity PendingIntent with correct mutability and back stack.
  • Full-screen intent: this is an exception for time-sensitive calling or alarm use cases, not engagement. Android 14 / target 34+ tightens USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT; check canUseFullScreenIntent() and provide a normal-notification fallback. Google Play eligibility and default-grant review are distribution policy, separate from the platform API.

Storage: ownership, collections, and durable access#

NeedDefault APILifetime / risk
Private app dataInternal filesDir/cacheDirNo permission; sandboxed; removed at uninstall. Cache can be evicted.
Large app-specific filesgetExternalFilesDir()No storage permission; volume can be unavailable; removed at uninstall.
App-created shared mediaMediaStore, RELATIVE_PATH, IS_PENDINGOwn inserts normally need no broad read permission; shared media survives uninstall. Editing or deleting others' content needs scoped consent.
User-selected photos/videosPhoto Picker / PickVisualMediaNo broad library permission; scoped URI grant. Persist when the contract supports it and still handle loss.
Arbitrary document, create, exportSAF: OPEN_DOCUMENT, CREATE_DOCUMENT, OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREEcontent:// document URI; request and take a persistable grant where needed; provider, reinstall, or user action can invalidate it.

Scoped storage is the default on Android 10 and enforced for apps targeting Android 11+; requestLegacyExternalStorage is ignored at target 30+. Before the target upgrade, a legacy app must migrate into app-specific storage, MediaStore, or a user-chosen SAF location. Make migration resumable and idempotent, and retain the source until the copy is verified.

File paths and document URIs are not interchangeable. Do not turn content:// into a guessed /storage/... path. Use ContentResolver, streams or file descriptors, and MIME/display-name metadata. Even where MediaStore supports a direct path for particular media cases, that is not a universal SAF, cloud, or provider property.

MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is broad special access for narrow core use cases, not a shortcut. Platform access and Google Play approval remain separate requirements.

Package visibility, URI grants, and FileProvider#

  • Android 11 / target 30+ filters package query results. Declare narrow <queries> entries for packages, intents, or providers. QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is a rare special case subject to Play approval. “Not found” can mean invisible rather than uninstalled.
  • Share a private file using FileProvider with narrowly whitelisted paths, a content:// URI, FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION or write permission, and ClipData for every URI. Do not expose a broad root or use file://.
  • A URI permission is a capability token for a resource, mode, and lifetime. Validate scheme, authority, MIME, and size; handle SecurityException and FileNotFoundException; do not log sensitive URIs; revoke temporary grants where appropriate.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Safe claimDo not promise
The system returns the current grant check for a permission.The grant remains unchanged until next launch, or rationale=false definitively means permanent denial.
Activity Result Registry can deliver a pending result after recreation with correct registration.An old View or in-memory request context survives process death, or the callback matches the desired business state.
A channel preserves user-controlled settings.The app can raise user-lowered importance or guarantee heads-up/full-screen delivery.
A persistable SAF grant can survive process and reboot.The URI is eternal, is a file path, survives reinstall, or cloud content is always local.
Platform APIs have documented OS and target gates.Google Play approval or identical behavior across every OEM UI, power, and privacy layer.

Version timeline / targetSdk matrix#

OS/APIKey changeGate / upgrade caveat
6 / 23Dangerous permissions become runtime.The runtime model depended on target 23+; always test the current target.
8 / 26Notification channels.Without a channel, notifications do not post for target 26+; user settings persist.
10 / 29Scoped storage default; separate background location.A temporary legacy opt-out existed; background requires manifest plus runtime grant.
11 / 30One-time permissions, auto-reset, package visibility, and stricter background-location sequence.Scoped storage enforced at target 30; requestLegacyExternalStorage ignored.
12 / 31Approximate location, Nearby Bluetooth, and notification-trampoline restriction.Many changes activate at target 31; precision downgrade can restart the process.
13 / 33POST_NOTIFICATIONS, granular media, Nearby Wi‑Fi, and system Photo Picker.Fresh install differs from eligible OS upgrade or pre-grant; old-target prompt timing differs.
14 / 34Selected Photos Access and tighter full-screen intents.Implement reselection when owning media-permission UX; check special access at runtime.
15–16 / 35–36Privacy and security continue evolving, including granular health permissions at Android 16.Read both “all apps” and “targeting N” docs; Play target API deadlines are separate and change over time.

A release matrix separates device OS, targetSdk, fresh install/restore/OS upgrade, and app update. Do not branch only on SDK_INT: manifest maxSdkVersion, target-gated behavior, current user state, and store policy also matter.

Decision framework#

  1. Name user value and data: exact resource or action, sensitivity, retention, sharing, and deletion.
  2. Find a permissionless API: picker, SAF, app-specific storage, own MediaStore write, or CDM before broad access.
  3. Build a capability matrix: OS × target × manifest × grant/scope × lifecycle × store policy; define degraded mode.
  4. Ask contextually: after explicit action, in separate stages, without dark patterns; show rationale only when useful.
  5. Use defence in depth: check immediately before use, handle revocation, partial result, and exceptions; minimize persistence and telemetry.
  6. Verify transitions: fresh, upgrade, restore, denial, auto-reset, process recreation, channel settings, URI loss, plus named OEM observations.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • A broad permission simplifies queries but increases privacy blast radius, denial rate, and policy cost; picker or SAF adds URI lifetime and provider failure.
  • A pre-prompt can give context but another modal before the system dialog creates friction. Never disguise denial as mandatory when degraded mode exists.
  • A cached “granted=true” becomes stale; permission, channel, and URI access can change outside the app. Checking only in onboarding is a production defect.
  • One channel for everything couples transactional and marketing opt-out; too many channels overload settings. Semantics and stable IDs are a product contract.
  • A persisted URI without metadata and validation fails after provider removal, user move, expiry, or reinstall; copied files without retention create privacy debt.
  • A target SDK bump can activate several changes together. Inventory manifests and APIs, stage rollout, test compatibility, and keep data migrations rollback-safe.

Production scenario: chat attachment, nearby device, and alerts#

Hypothetically: a chat attachment uses Photo Picker, stores URI plus MIME and size, and copies only when offline resend or retention requires it. Upload reads through ContentResolver, catches a lost grant, and asks for reselection rather than crashing. Camera permission is requested only after a camera tap, while text and file flows still work. Nearby pairing evaluates CDM first; otherwise it uses versioned Bluetooth permissions and legacy maxSdkVersion.

Delivery alerts use a transactional channel separate from marketing. The app asks for POST_NOTIFICATIONS after alert opt-in, exposes an in-app inbox after denial, and never recreates a channel to raise importance. A call-style full-screen path exists only for a real incoming call, checks special access, and falls back to heads-up or in-app UI. Analytics records transition category and feature outcome, never URI, location, or content.

Code-review/debugging trap#

if (!shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(READ_MEDIA_IMAGES)) {
    openSettings() // BUG: also false before first request
}
val path = selectedUri.path!!
File(path).copyTo(uploadFile) // BUG: a document URI is not a filesystem path

notificationManager.createNotificationChannel(
    NotificationChannel("orders", "Orders", IMPORTANCE_HIGH)
) // does not override the user's lower importance

Review should find three independent defects: an incomplete denial oracle, URI/path confusion, and a channel assumption. Then inspect request history, current checkSelfPermission, partial-media scope, persistable grant and stream closure, size/MIME bounds, process recreation, app/channel state, and target-specific manifest. Fix with explicit UI state plus current capability check; ContentResolver.openInputStream/openFileDescriptor; and respect for channel settings, linking to Settings only after user action.

Test matrix and adb/debug techniques#

AxisMinimum cases
OS / targetAPI 23, 29/30, 31/32, 33, 34, and current 35/36; legacy target only for migration, current target for release.
Install pathFresh install, app update with target bump, OS upgrade, backup/restore, reinstall.
PermissionNever asked, allow, deny once/twice, Settings revoke, one-time expiry, auto-reset, coarse-only, foreground-only, selected photos and reselection.
NotificationApp denial, channel NONE/LOW/HIGH, user-lowered importance, DND, eligible/ineligible upgrade, trampoline tap, full-screen fallback.

adb shell pm list permissions -d -g
adb shell pm grant com.example.app android.permission.CAMERA
adb shell pm revoke com.example.app android.permission.CAMERA
adb shell pm clear-permission-flags com.example.app android.permission.CAMERA user-set user-fixed
adb shell pm revoke com.example.app android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS
adb shell pm clear-permission-flags com.example.app android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS user-set user-fixed
adb shell dumpsys package com.example.app
adb shell cmd appops get com.example.app
adb shell dumpsys notification --noredact
adb shell am kill com.example.app
adb shell am force-stop com.example.app

Commands and flags vary by API and build, so record the emulator image or device. Use documented page-specific commands for auto-reset, hibernation, and compatibility changes on that version, then restore state. UI tests cannot safely replace system dialogs with brittle app selectors; establish preconditions through shell/test APIs and assert app state after the system result.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Why is permission a state machine? There is app-owned never-requested state, denied with rationale, blocked-like denial, temporary or partial scope, and granted. State changes outside the app, so every use re-checks.
  2. Does rationale=false mean “don't ask again”? No. It is not a complete permanent-denial oracle: it is also false before the first request and under other platform or policy states. Combine request history with current grant without claiming certainty.
  3. How does Activity Result API survive recreation? The registry stores pending results. Register launchers unconditionally in stable order and reconstruct business intent from saved or durable state.
  4. How do you request background location? Foreground coarse/fine first; background is a separate education and Settings flow on Android 11+, only for a core case and separately from Play approval.
  5. What changed for Bluetooth and media? Android 12 introduced granular Nearby Bluetooth; Android 13 added Nearby Wi‑Fi and split media; Android 14 added selected visual media. Use a versioned manifest and per-permission checks.
  6. What does notification permission mean? It is an app-level gate from API 33; channel and user state are additional gates. The FGS notification obligation remains after denial.
  7. Why not raise channel importance? Channel settings persist and belong to the user. The app cannot override user-lowered importance and must not use a new ID to evade that choice.
  8. MediaStore, SAF, or Photo Picker? MediaStore for media collections and own writes; SAF for user-chosen arbitrary documents and trees; Photo Picker for scoped visual selection without broad library access.
  9. Why is uri.path not a file? A content:// URI is a provider capability and may be remote or virtual. Read through ContentResolver; file paths and document URIs are not interchangeable.
  10. How do you separate platform from OEM and Play? Name the official Android contract and target gate, then identify store eligibility and named OEM observations separately without universal claims.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. A result callback arrives after process recreation, but its upload target is gone. Do not execute an old lambda assumption. Read operation ID from SavedStateHandle or DB, revalidate URI and grant, then continue or ask the user to reselect.
  2. The user grants approximate location, but routing needs precision. Show a coarse result or degraded UX first. Request precision upgrade only after an explicit action and concrete value; denial must not block the whole app.
  3. After target 34, users see only some photos. Inventory manifest and grants, implement selected-media reselection or move to Photo Picker, remove cached full-library assumptions, and test app update paths.
  4. A critical notification does not appear heads-up. Inspect POST_NOTIFICATIONS, app and channel blocks, user-lowered importance, DND, and payload. Do not raise importance; offer user-driven Settings and an in-app fallback. Full-screen is only for a lawful call or alarm.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Which states does your permission reducer distinguish, and what evidence proves each state?
  2. Which permissionless API can replace the broadest grant in your app?
  3. What happens to the pending request, URI, and UI after process death and Settings revocation?
  4. Which OS × target × install-path combinations are critical for your next target SDK upgrade?
  5. Where does your documentation separate Android guarantees from Google Play policy and named OEM observations?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design permissions, storage, and notifications across Android versions?

~30-second answer#

I model permission as a revocable capability, not a dialog or cached Boolean. I first choose a permissionless API such as Photo Picker, SAF, or app-specific storage. Otherwise I request contextually through Activity Result APIs, handle denial, one-time and partial scope, and re-check immediately before use. I version behavior by both OS and target SDK. For notifications I respect the app grant and persistent user-owned channel importance. For storage I keep content URIs distinct from file paths. I test fresh installs, upgrades, recreation, Settings changes, URI loss, and named OEM devices without claiming universal OEM behavior.

~2-minute answer#

I begin with data minimization: the exact user value, resource, sensitivity, retention, and deletion semantics. Then I look for a system-mediated, permissionless API—Photo Picker for selected visual media, SAF for documents, MediaStore for app-owned shared media, or app-specific storage for private data.

When a dangerous permission is required, I model observable states rather than treating the result as a Boolean. A rationale false value is not a complete permanent-denial oracle. I combine the current grant with app-owned request history, support denial and Settings recovery without loops, and represent one-time, while-in-use, approximate, background, and selected-media scopes explicitly. Permissions can change outside the app, so every sensitive operation re-checks and handles failure. Activity Result launchers register unconditionally in stable order so pending results survive recreation; business intent lives in saved or durable state.

I maintain an OS-and-target matrix: Android 11 changed one-time grants, auto-reset, package visibility, and background-location flow; Android 12 added approximate location, Nearby Bluetooth, and notification-trampoline restrictions; Android 13 added notification permission, granular media, Nearby Wi-Fi, and Photo Picker; Android 14 added selected-photo access and tighter full-screen intent rules. Store policy is a separate gate.

Notification channels are persistent user-owned settings, so the app cannot raise importance the user lowered. Storage code treats content URIs as provider capabilities, never guessed paths, and validates persisted grants. Finally I test fresh install, app and OS upgrades, restore, partial and denied states, process death, channel overrides, provider loss, and current target SDK images, with OEM findings reported only for the tested device and firmware.

Kotlin Coroutines: foundations and internalsexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage, you should be able to explain a coroutine without calling it a “lightweight thread,” read its context and Job tree, choose a scope, dispatcher, and builder, make blocking or callback APIs main-safe and cancellable, and diagnose ownership, confinement, and cancellation defects. Detailed failure propagation, exception handling, and coroutine testing belong to Stage 8.

Senior mental model#

A coroutine is not a thread; it is an owned computation with a lifecycle and context. It occupies a thread only while executing, may suspend without blocking that thread, then may continue inline or be dispatched. The scope expresses ownership, the Job forms the lifetime tree, and the dispatcher decides where a runnable continuation may execute. suspend does not automatically move work off main.

  • Suspension: save the logical continuation and return control to the caller; the underlying thread can do other work.
  • Blocking: the thread cannot do other work until the API returns; wrapping a blocking call in a coroutine does not make it non-blocking.
  • Thread switching: a separate dispatcher or API decision. Suspension may complete without a switch, and resumption may be inline or queued.
  • Structured ownership: work has a parent and bounded lifetime; this does not guarantee database transactions, exactly-once network effects, or business atomicity.

Internals: Continuation, state machine, and context#

Suspend transformation mental model#

A useful model is that the compiler transforms a suspend function into continuation-passing form with an extra Continuation<T>; generated state retains a program counter and only the live locals needed around possible suspension points. A call either returns immediately or returns a suspended marker, and the continuation later receives a result or failure through resumeWith. This is a mental model, not a promise about generated class names, allocation counts, or bytecode shape: compiler backends may optimize it.

// Source
suspend fun profile(id: UserId): Profile {
    val local = cache.read(id)       // may complete inline
    return local ?: api.fetch(id)    // may suspend
}

// Conceptual only, not source/API-compatible generated code:
fun profile(id: UserId, completion: Continuation<Profile>): Any? =
    stateMachine(id, completion)

Continuation.context carries CoroutineContext. A context is an indexed set of elements such as a Job, dispatcher, CoroutineName, and thread-context elements. left + right combines it; an element on the right replaces an element with the same key. It is not an ordered interceptor pipeline.

Scope, Job tree, launch/async, and boundaries#

  • CoroutineScope is an owner plus a coroutineContext, not merely a launch utility. A custom long-lived scope needs an explicit owner, Job, dispatcher, shutdown point, and observability.
  • A child Job belongs to its parent; parent completion waits for children, and parent cancellation propagates downward. Exact failure and supervision rules are Stage 8.
  • launch returns a Job: use it for concurrent work whose value is not returned. async returns Deferred<T>: use it when a concurrent result will be awaited. async { x() }.await() immediately adds overhead without concurrency.
  • coroutineScope creates a structured boundary and returns after its children finish. supervisorScope creates a supervisory boundary with different sibling ownership; detailed failure behavior and handler rules are reserved for Stage 8.

Dispatchers, withContext, and confinement#

ToolUseBoundary / caveat
Dispatchers.MainAndroid UI access and short UI-state work.Requires the platform Main dispatcher; no blocking I/O or long CPU loop.
Main.immediateAvoid an extra dispatch when already on the matching main context.May resume inline and change reentrancy or ordering assumptions; otherwise dispatches. Support is platform-specific.
DefaultCPU-bound work on bounded shared parallelism.Parallel work is not automatically faster; chunking, cancellation checks, contention, and measurement matter.
IOBlocking I/O that cannot be made suspending.Uses shared elastic resources; it is not “one new thread per coroutine” or permission for unbounded downstream load.
limitedParallelism(n)A dispatcher view limiting concurrent execution for a subsystem.Not a dedicated thread, durable queue, fairness SLA, or external resource pool. Use n=1 for sequential execution, not thread identity.

withContext(context) merges the supplied context, runs the block, and returns its result while retaining structured ownership. A changed dispatcher normally dispatches to it and back, but there is no universal thread-switch guarantee: equivalent or immediate contexts may execute inline. Inject dispatchers at boundaries so blocking and CPU implementation details are main-safe and testable.

Cooperative cancellation and cleanup#

Cancellation is cooperative. Cancellable suspending functions check it; a CPU loop or blocking API that never suspends must poll ensureActive(), use yield() where yielding is actually desired, or call an interruptible/cancellable adapter. yield() is not a scheduler fairness guarantee or a performance fix.

suspend fun index(rows: List<Row>): Index = withContext(cpuDispatcher) {
    buildIndex {
        rows.forEachIndexed { i, row ->
            if (i % 256 == 0) ensureActive()
            add(row)
        }
    }
}

try {
    sync()
} finally {
    withContext(NonCancellable) { closeSession() } // short suspending cleanup only
}

finally performs ordinary non-suspending cleanup. Use NonCancellable only for bounded suspending cleanup that must finish after cancellation; it does not create an independent background lifetime. It does not replace timeout, retry, or compensating business effects.

Android ownership: ViewModel, Lifecycle, and collection#

  • viewModelScope owns screen or business work that should survive configuration changes and is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared. A repository exposes main-safe suspend APIs; it must not smuggle UI work into GlobalScope.
  • lifecycleScope is cancelled when its Lifecycle is destroyed. For Fragment View UI, use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope, not the Fragment lifetime for stale bindings.
  • repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) suspends its caller, launches the block while at least STARTED, cancels that block below STARTED, and restarts it on re-entry. Launch independent collectors as children in the block; sequential collect calls do not run concurrently.
  • A real application scope can be injected for app-lifetime work, but it needs a documented owner, shutdown, and error policy. Avoid GlobalScope and per-call CoroutineScope(...), which hide cancellation and outlive the caller.

Callback bridging, runBlocking, and context propagation#

suspend fun LocationClient.awaitFix(): Fix = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    val callback = object : Callback {
        override fun onFix(value: Fix) {
            stop(this)
            if (cont.isActive) cont.resume(value) // API must have one terminal path
        }
        override fun onError(t: Throwable) {
            stop(this)
            if (cont.isActive) cont.resumeWithException(t)
        }
    }
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { stop(callback) }
    start(callback)
}

The adapter needs an atomic, single terminal protocol: callback code resumes the continuation at most once, cancellation unregisters and releases resources, a synchronous callback during registration is safe, and a late callback is ignored or disposed. suspendCancellableCoroutine has a prompt cancellation guarantee: if the Job is cancelled before a dispatched resumption runs, the coroutine does not continue successfully, so a transferred resource needs a cancellation disposer. isActive alone is not atomic protection against two racing callbacks; prefer upstream unregister or an atomic guard and overloads that define resource cleanup.

runBlocking bridges blocking callers by blocking the current thread while it runs an event loop. Use it at process entry points and narrow legacy or test boundaries—not inside suspend code, Android main callbacks, repositories, or servers where it can starve or deadlock constrained executors.

A coroutine may resume on another thread; raw ThreadLocal values do not automatically follow it. Prefer explicit context parameters. Where a legacy library requires it, use ThreadLocal.asContextElement(value) and understand that it propagates a context value, not arbitrary in-coroutine mutations; MDC and copyable-context behavior are library- and version-specific.

Guarantees versus non-guarantees#

Safe claimDo not promise
Suspension can release a thread for other work; a coroutine has a context and Job.A coroutine is a thread, or every suspension changes threads.
suspend permits suspension points.suspend automatically makes a blocking API non-blocking or moves work off main.
A structured scope waits for owned children and propagates cancellation through its Job tree.The business operation became atomic, durable, or exactly once.
A cancellation signal and cancellable suspension support cooperative stopping.Arbitrary CPU, native, or blocking code stops immediately.
A dispatcher defines execution policy for continuations.A specific thread, queue fairness, order of all resumptions, or inline/dispatch behavior in every case.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Pin Kotlin, kotlinx-coroutines-core, kotlinx-coroutines-android, and AndroidX Lifecycle versions; check API documentation for the resolved version.
  • Dispatchers.Main on Android comes from the integration module; Main.immediate semantics and support depend on the platform dispatcher.
  • limitedParallelism, debugging APIs, test schedulers, and thread-context facilities evolve. Do not carry snippets across major or minor versions without migration notes.
  • DebugProbes and debug-agent capabilities may be experimental or version-sensitive and have overhead; production enablement requires a separate decision.

Decision framework#

  1. Define owner and lifetime: caller, ViewModel, View lifecycle, application, or durable scheduler?
  2. Classify the work: suspending I/O, blocking I/O, CPU, UI mutation, or callback bridge.
  3. Choose the API: sequential suspend by default; launch for owned no-result work; async only for a concurrent value.
  4. Place the boundary: main-safe implementation with an injected dispatcher; concurrency limit tied to the real bottleneck.
  5. Design cancellation and cleanup: suspension checks, loop polling, unregister or close, and bounded NonCancellable.
  6. Verify semantics: ownership tree, resumption and reentrancy, thread-local assumptions, logs and traces, process death, and business idempotency outside coroutine guarantees.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • Extra async and dispatcher hops can increase allocations, queues, and latency; sequential code is often clearer and faster.
  • IO prevents main-thread blocking, but unbounded requests can still exhaust sockets, database connections, or vendor quotas; limit according to downstream capacity.
  • Main.immediate removes a hop, but inline reentrancy can violate “callback happens later” assumptions.
  • limitedParallelism(1) serializes tasks on a dispatcher view but does not provide a durable queue, process safety, thread affinity, or database transaction.
  • Broad NonCancellable hides shutdown and hangs teardown; missing callback unregister leaks owners and permits late double resume.
  • Coroutines reduce waiting cost, not CPU complexity, memory retention, lock contention, or network latency. Measure traces and queueing before claiming performance.

Production scenario: checkout orchestration#

Hypothetically: CheckoutViewModel owns a viewModelScope.launch. Repository APIs are main-safe: remote suspending calls remain sequential until genuine parallelism is required; legacy receipt parsing uses an injected Default.limitedParallelism(2), and a blocking SDK call is isolated with injected IO capacity. Two independent quotes use sibling async values inside coroutineScope and both are awaited.

The UI collects state with viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope and repeatOnLifecycle. A payment SDK callback is wrapped with suspendCancellableCoroutine, one atomic terminal decision, unregister-on-cancel, and late-token disposal. Cancellation stops UI ownership but does not claim that a remote charge was rolled back: payment uses an idempotency key, durable operation record, server status query, and reconciliation. That transaction protocol is outside structured-concurrency guarantees.

Code-review/debugging trap#

fun refresh() {
    CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { // hidden owner; never cancelled
        val dto = api.load()                // suspend does not prove blocking safety
        withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) { render(dto) }
    }
}

suspend fun awaitSdk() = suspendCancellableCoroutine<Result> { c ->
    sdk.start { c.resume(it) }              // no unregister; callback may fire twice
}

Review questions: who owns the Job and where is shutdown; is api.load actually main-safe; why manually hop to Main instead of updating owned state; can inline Main.immediate cause reentrancy; what does cancellation do; does the callback have a single terminal protocol? Debug with CoroutineName, the IDE Coroutines view, -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug in a non-production diagnostic run, job-tree or log correlation, and traces around the blocking call. Debug probes can expose suspended stacks, but they do not prove business ownership or exactly-once behavior.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. Is a coroutine a lightweight thread? No. It is a computation with a continuation, context, and Job that executes on threads according to dispatcher policy; many coroutines can share threads.
  2. What does suspend actually mean? The function may suspend and later resume its continuation; the modifier does not guarantee a background thread, non-blocking implementation, or thread switch.
  3. How should you picture compiler transformation? As a continuation-passing state machine with a label and live locals near suspension points, without promising exact generated classes or allocations.
  4. How is CoroutineContext composed? It contains keyed elements; left + right replaces an element with the same key. Job defines lifetime and a dispatcher defines execution policy.
  5. launch or async? Use launch for owned no-result work and async when a concurrently produced value is awaited. Immediate await usually means sequential suspension was better.
  6. coroutineScope or supervisorScope? Both bound children and await completion; the supervisor boundary changes sibling failure ownership. Detailed propagation belongs to Stage 8.
  7. Default, IO, or Main? Main for short UI access, Default for CPU work, and IO for unavoidable blocking I/O; inject them and limit according to downstream capacity.
  8. How does cancellation work? Cooperatively: cancellable suspension observes it; CPU loops call ensureActive or yield deliberately; cleanup uses finally and narrowly bounded NonCancellable when it must suspend.
  9. How do you bridge a callback? Use suspendCancellableCoroutine, an at-most-one terminal resume, unregister on cancellation, safe synchronous registration, and late resource cleanup.
  10. What does structured concurrency not guarantee? It bounds lifetime and joins children, but does not provide transaction atomicity, durability, remote rollback, or exactly-once effects.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. withContext(IO) is called from IO. Do not promise a switch: the implementation may continue without a meaningful hop. Correctness comes from execution policy, not a thread-name assertion.
  2. A mutable engine needs single-threaded access. limitedParallelism(1) gives sequential execution but not one stable thread. If the library requires thread identity, use and document an appropriate owned dispatcher or executor and close it.
  3. A callback returns a resource concurrently with cancellation. Design an atomic terminal hand-off and cancellation disposer; an isActive check alone races.
  4. The user leaves during payment. Cancel UI ownership, but reconcile remote status using a durable operation ID and idempotency key; coroutine cancellation is not payment rollback.

5 self-check questions without answers#

  1. Draw the Job tree for one screen flow: who owns it, and where does every child end?
  2. Which suspend APIs in your codebase may still block main?
  3. Where could Main.immediate or a synchronous callback cause reentrancy?
  4. How does your callback bridge prove at-most-once resume and cleanup after cancellation?
  5. Which business effect needs idempotency or a transaction beyond structured concurrency?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do Kotlin coroutines work, and how do you choose their ownership and execution context?

~30-second answer#

A coroutine is not a thread. It is an owned computation represented through continuations and a context containing elements such as a Job and dispatcher. Suspension releases control but does not automatically move work off main; resumption may be inline or dispatched. I choose the owner first, keep APIs main-safe, use Main for UI, Default for CPU work and IO for unavoidable blocking calls, and make cancellation and callback cleanup cooperative. Structured concurrency bounds child lifetimes, but it does not make business effects atomic or exactly once.

~2-minute answer#

My mental model starts with the compiler converting a suspend function into continuation-passing code, typically a state machine around suspension points. That is a useful model, not a bytecode-shape guarantee. A coroutine runs on a thread only while executing; suspension is different from blocking, and suspend does not imply an IO dispatcher or any thread switch.

I choose ownership before concurrency. A scope carries a context, its Job forms a parent-child tree, and a structured boundary waits for owned children. I use launch for no-result owned work and async only when I need a concurrently produced value. CoroutineScope and supervisorScope both define boundaries; detailed failure propagation is a separate policy discussion.

Dispatchers are execution policies: Main for short UI work, Default for CPU work, IO for unavoidable blocking I/O. Main.immediate may run inline and limitedParallelism is a view limiting concurrency, not a dedicated thread or durable queue. withContext merges context and returns a result; it does not universally guarantee a switch.

Cancellation is cooperative, so CPU loops check ensureActive and callback adapters unregister on cancellation with a single terminal resume protocol. Android work is owned by viewModelScope or the appropriate Lifecycle, and repeatOnLifecycle restarts collection with visibility. I avoid GlobalScope and ad-hoc scopes. Finally, I separate coroutine guarantees from business guarantees: remote writes still need idempotency, persistence, and reconciliation, and I use coroutine names, IDE tooling, and traces to debug ownership and blocking.
