Advanced Kotlin Flow in productionexpand / collapse

Learning objective#

After this stage you should be able to design a production Flow topology: select timing, order, and completion semantics for composition and flattening; build latest-wins search without stale state; localize failure and retry; own sharing lifecycle and cache boundaries; integrate callbacks; and prove timing, cancellation, retry, and sharing with deterministic tests. Stage 9 basics and Stage 10 primitives appear only as comparative context.

Senior mental model#

A Flow topology is executable policy. For every edge, name ownership, ordering, concurrency, buffering, cancellation, failure, restart, and durability. An operator cannot repair the wrong business contract: latest-wins, all-results, paired-results, and durable work are different requirements.

  • A cold chain runs per collector; a hot boundary moves execution into its owner scope. Collector lifecycle and producer lifecycle are separate decisions.
  • Cancellation is control flow, not rollback. latest operators cancel cooperatively and cannot retract an HTTP request, database commit, or other external side effect.
  • Errors either terminate a stream or become typed domain values. Choose explicitly at a layer boundary.

Internals and operator topology#

source(s) → admission/rate policy → composition/flattening → error policy
          → context/buffer boundary → domain state → stateIn/shareIn(owner scope)
          → repeatOnLifecycle collector → render

Sequential operators normally execute in the collector coroutine. buffer, flowOn, flattening, channelFlow, and sharing may introduce channels or coroutines. Read data left-to-right, cancellation and failures right-to-left, and mark every external effect.

combine vs zip vs merge; flattening and latest transforms#

OperatorTiming/orderCompletion/failure
combineAfter its initial barrier, transforms latest values whenever any input changes.combine waits for the first value from every input. A completed input can retain its latest value while others emit; a failure terminates composition.
zipPairs the n-th values; a faster side waits/buffers under the contract.Completes when one side can form no more pairs and cancels remaining collection; failures propagate.
mergeCollects inputs concurrently and interleaves ready values without cross-input order.Normally completes after all inputs; an unhandled failure terminates merge and cancels siblings.
  • flatMapConcat collects inner flows sequentially and preserves outer order, with head-of-line blocking.
  • flatMapMerge(concurrency = n) collects up to n inners; output ordering follows timing. The limit is resource policy, not a business order or rate limit.
  • flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner; mapLatest cancels its previous transform; transformLatest can emit multiple values and cancels the whole previous block.
  • Use latest only when old work is obsolete. Use concat or bounded merge when every result matters.

Search pipeline: latest cancellation and stale-result protection#

val results: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = query
    .map(String::trim).debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { q ->
        if (q.length < 2) flowOf(SearchUiState.Idle)
        else flow<SearchUiState> {
            emit(SearchUiState.Loading(q))
            emit(SearchUiState.Content(q, repository.search(q)))
        }.catch { e ->
            if (e is CancellationException) throw e
            emit(SearchUiState.Error(q, e.toDomainError()))
        }
    }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState.Idle)
  • debounce is quiet-time admission; distinctUntilChanged removes adjacent equal normalized queries. Neither is caching.
  • For a blocking, uncancellable, or detached API, carry a request generation/query key into the reducer and reject a mismatched result.
  • Cancellation cannot undo a server mutation; writes need idempotency and reconciliation, not latest-wins.

Multi-source UI state and initial-emission traps#

  • Use combine for latest account, rows, and filter state when any source should rerender. Model initial/loading/absent/error explicitly.
  • A change-only callback, filtered source, or SharedFlow(replay=0) may never provide the first value, so combine may emit nothing. Seed only with a truthful initial state.
  • Independent latest values are not an atomic multi-source transaction. Read a database transaction or one versioned aggregate when consistency requires it.
  • One unhandled input failure terminates the aggregate. Materialize recoverable per-source errors before combine only when partial UI is required.

Exception transparency, completion, and retry boundaries#

  • catch handles upstream exceptions and preserves cancellation; catch does not catch downstream collector failures. An onEach before catch is in its recovery scope; one after catch is downstream.
  • onCompletion { cause } observes normal completion, failure, or cancellation and does not suppress failure. It is not catch.
  • retry/retryWhen re-subscribes and may repeat builders, calls, and side effects. Retry only typed transient failures with bounded attempts; never retry cancellation, programmer defects, authentication/authorization, validation, or deterministic client errors.
  • Use capped exponential backoff, jitter, connectivity policy, and a total deadline. Inject clock/randomness in tests and honor bounded server retry guidance.
  • Rethrow CancellationException. Materialize expected domain failures as sealed values if the stream should continue; terminate on invariants/programmer errors.

stateIn/shareIn lifecycle, cache, and single source of truth#

  • The supplied scope owns stateIn/shareIn. Match it to data lifetime; do not hide it in a global scope.
  • Eagerly starts now, Lazily starts once, and WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis, replayExpirationMillis) can stop, expire state/replay, and restart. Subscriber gaps can repeat setup or side effects.
  • Place catch/retry/completion policy before sharing. Normal upstream completion does not complete hot subscribers; an upstream exception is handled by the owner scope.
  • Hot-sharing replay is not a durable cache. It does not define freshness, persistence, invalidation, or the repository/database single source of truth.
  • Sharing provides no exactly-once network/database effect. Use idempotency, transactions/outbox, operation IDs, and reconciliation.

Context, fusion, buffers, concurrency, and partial results#

  • flowOn changes upstream context only and may create a channel across dispatchers; it cannot change collector context.
  • Adjacent channelFlow/callbackFlow, flowOn, buffer, and produceIn may fuse. Capacity, overflow, and placement change suspension, loss, and cancellation windows.
  • buffer overlaps producer and consumer; conflate drops intermediate values; latest cancels work. Place expensive transforms deliberately.
  • flatMapMerge bounds active inner collections, not all work those inners may spawn. Output order is not input order.
  • For independent partial failure, use supervisorScope outside Flow to create typed outcomes, then emit them. Merge is not a supervisor boundary.

callbackFlow and Android lifecycle re-subscription#

  • callbackFlow registers per collector, uses thread-safe trySend, and must unregister in awaitClose. Set buffering for the callback rate and inspect failed sends.
  • Make close/unregister races safe under the callback API. Cancellation cleans up but cannot undo callback side effects.
  • repeatOnLifecycle cancels and relaunches collection. A cold callback re-registers, and WhileSubscribed may restart after its timeout. Test start/stop counts.
  • Share in a longer owner only when multiple collectors should truly reuse one registration.

Guarantees vs non-guarantees#

GuaranteeNon-guarantee
combine uses latest after all first values; zip pairs; merge interleaves.Universal ordering, atomic snapshots, or an emission when a combine input never emits.
Latest requests cancellation of previous work.Preemption of blocking code or rollback of external effects.
Retry can re-subscribe conditionally.Safe repeats or exactly-once effects.
catch sees upstream non-cancellation failures.Downstream failures or cancellation are caught.
Sharing can replay in-memory values within its scope.Durable caching, invisible restart, or exactly-once network/database effects.

Version-sensitive behavior#

  • Latest/flattening/dynamic debounce and sharing APIs may have experimental or preview annotations in a resolved release. Inspect the pinned API.
  • Default merge concurrency and channel capacity can be library/property-sensitive; pass explicit values when operationally relevant.
  • WhileSubscribed overloads, Duration support, and replay-expiration annotations vary by release. Pin one coroutines family and test boundaries.
  • AndroidX lifecycle and Compose collection signatures/default states depend on the resolved AndroidX version; lifecycle is not durability.

Decision framework#

  1. Name the requirement: paired, latest snapshot, concurrent all-results, latest-wins, ordered work, or durable work.
  2. Write initial, completion, and failure behavior for every source.
  3. Choose cancellation/concurrency and classify every effect as idempotent, transactional, compensatable, or unsafe to repeat.
  4. Place context, buffers, catch/retry, and sharing; assign owner/start/expiration.
  5. Define source of truth, freshness, lifecycle re-subscription, telemetry, and a deterministic test timeline.

Trade-offs and failure modes#

  • combine is responsive but can recompute or wait forever; zip preserves pairing but stalls; merge improves concurrency with nondeterministic interleaving.
  • Latest removes stale cooperative work but drops progress; concat preserves order with latency; merge adds load, memory, and ordering costs.
  • Broad fallback catch hides incidents. Infinite broad retry amplifies outages and resource use.
  • Wrong sharing scope leaks; short timeout thrashes; long timeout retains resources; replay can be stale.
  • Lifecycle collection, retry, and sharing restart can multiply effects. Observe starts, attempts, cancellation, and operation IDs.

Production scenario: offline-first search#

Hypothetically: normalized query, account, and filters combine into a versioned request. Debounce/distinct/latest controls search. A database Flow is the single source of truth; refresh transactionally writes keyed network results. A generation guard rejects stale uncancellable completions. Bounded jittered retry handles transient I/O; auth and validation become domain state; cancellation is rethrown.

combine(query, filters, account) { q, f, a -> RequestKey(q.trim(), f, a.id) }
    .debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { key ->
        repository.observeRows(key)
            .onStart { repository.refresh(key) } // repeat-safe boundary required
            .retryWhen { e, attempt ->
                val retry = e is IOException && attempt < 3
                if (retry) delay(backoffWithJitter(attempt))
                retry
            }.catch { e ->
                if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                emit(emptyList()) // real code maps a typed domain error
            }
    }

The onStart refresh can repeat after retry or restart; production repository deduplication/idempotency owns it. There is no exactly-once network/database effect.

Code-review/debugging trap#

query.flatMapMerge { api.search(it) }          // stale results, unclear concurrency
    .catch { emit(emptyList()) }               // hides domain/programmer failures
    .retryWhen { _, _ -> true }                // repeats forever
    .shareIn(GlobalScope, Eagerly, replay = 1) // leaked owner; not persistence

Ask which result wins, what happens before first values, what can repeat, whether cancellation is preserved, who owns sharing, and where durable truth lives. Trace request ID, key, attempt, upstream start/stop, subscriber count, cancellation cause, latency, drops, and lifecycle state without logging secrets.

Deterministic testing and observability#

  • Use one runTest and shared TestCoroutineScheduler across injected test dispatchers; advance exact virtual-time boundaries.
  • Assert combine's barrier/latest snapshots, zip pairing/early completion, merge membership without false global order, and failure cancellation.
  • Make the old latest inner suspend, observe its finally, advance debounce exactly, reject stale output, and count retry subscriptions/effects/backoff.
  • For sharing, count starts/stops, cross timeout and replayExpirationMillis, resubscribe, cancel owner, and verify callback cleanup under lifecycle.
  • Telemetry distinguishes requested, admitted, started, cancelled, retried, succeeded, materialized error, stale-rejected, dropped, and rendered.

10 likely practice Q&A#

These are likely practice questions, not a confirmed or guaranteed interview list.

  1. combine, zip, or merge? combine produces latest snapshots after all first values; zip forms positional pairs and ends with the shorter side; merge interleaves concurrent inputs.
  2. Which flattening operator? concat for ordered all-results, bounded merge for concurrent all-results, latest when previous intent is obsolete.
  3. Why can search still become stale? Blocking, uncancellable, or detached work can complete externally; carry a generation/key and reject mismatches.
  4. Where should catch go? After the operators it owns and before its materialization/sharing boundary; it does not catch downstream collectors.
  5. What does onCompletion do? Observes normal, failed, or cancelled termination; it does not recover failure.
  6. When is retry safe? For classified transient failures with bounded backoff/jitter/deadline and repeat-safe upstream, never auth/validation/bugs/cancellation.
  7. Why can WhileSubscribed duplicate I/O? A new subscriber restarts a stopped cold upstream; choose owner/timeout and idempotent setup.
  8. Is replay a cache? It is only in-memory replay, not durable storage, freshness policy, or source of truth.
  9. How do partial results work? Materialize per-source outcomes; use supervisorScope outside Flow for independent concurrent failure isolation.
  10. How do you test timing? runTest with one scheduler, controlled fakes, explicit virtual-time steps, and cancellation/subscription/attempt assertions.

4 senior follow-ups with answers#

  1. A combine input completed after a value. Its latest can continue combining with other inputs; decide whether that stale completed dimension is acceptable.
  2. One user action caused three POSTs. Retry re-subscribed. Use an idempotency key and reconciliation or retry only a safe read.
  3. Rotation reconnects a callback twice. Trace repeatOnLifecycle, stop timeout, and owner; make register/unregister symmetric and test subscribers.
  4. You need input order and concurrency. Add sequence IDs and an explicit reordering aggregator, or use concat when latency permits.

5 unanswered self-checks#

  1. What are each source's initial, completion, and error contracts if it never emits?
  2. Where does cooperative cancellation end, and what stale guard remains?
  3. Which effects can retry, re-subscription, or sharing restart repeat?
  4. Who owns hot scope, replay lifetime, source of truth, and invalidation?
  5. What virtual timeline proves debounce, cancellation, retry, and replay expiration?

Interview-ready English answer skeletons#

Question: How do you design a production Kotlin Flow pipeline?

~30-second answer#

I treat a Flow chain as an execution policy. I use combine for latest snapshots after every input emits, zip for pairs, and merge for unordered concurrent values. Search normalizes, debounces, deduplicates, and uses flatMapLatest plus a stale request guard because cancellation is cooperative. I classify failures before bounded retry, preserve cancellation, and scope catch upstream. Sharing has an explicit owner and start strategy; replay is not durable cache. runTest with one scheduler verifies timing, cancellation, retries, restart, and lifecycle re-subscription.

~2-minute answer#

I first name the required semantics: positional pairs, latest snapshot, concurrent all-results, latest-wins, ordered work, or durable work. combine waits for every first value, zip pairs and ends with the shorter side, and merge interleaves. flatMapConcat preserves order, flatMapMerge bounds concurrent inner flows, and latest variants cooperatively cancel old work.

For search I normalize, debounce, deduplicate, and flatMapLatest. Cancellation cannot roll back a request, commit, blocking call, or detached job, so I carry a request key and reject stale completion. Multi-source UI models truthful initial/loading/error values; independent latest values are not an atomic transaction.

catch handles upstream non-cancellation failures, not downstream collectors. onCompletion observes but does not recover. retryWhen re-subscribes and can repeat effects, so only typed transient failures receive bounded capped backoff, jitter, and a total deadline; cancellation, auth, validation, and programmer errors do not. Expected domain errors may become values.

stateIn/shareIn belongs to a named scope. Eagerly, Lazily, and WhileSubscribed differ in start, stop, replay expiration, and restart, so upstream setup must tolerate repetition. Replay is memory, not durable cache or source of truth. flowOn and buffer placement changes concurrency and may fuse with callbackFlow; awaitClose owns callback cleanup. repeatOnLifecycle re-subscribes. Tests use one TestCoroutineScheduler and assert exact emissions, cancellation, attempts, starts/stops, replay reset, and callback cleanup. Observability records request IDs, attempts, cancellation causes, and lifecycle. Exactly-once network/database effects require idempotency and transactional reconciliation outside Flow.

Kotlin for Androidexpand / collapse

val vs var and immutability#

val means the reference is read-only; it does not guarantee deep immutability. var means the reference can be reassigned. In Android UI state, immutability makes state predictable and easier to test.

data class CheckoutUiState(
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val items: List<CartItemUi> = emptyList(),
    val error: UiError? = null
)

Senior note#

Mutable state should be owned by one component. ViewModel can own a private MutableStateFlow, while UI observes public StateFlow.

private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutUiState())
val uiState: StateFlow<CheckoutUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

Nullability, lateinit, and lazy#

Kotlin null-safety helps model absence explicitly. Avoid !! in production code unless you can prove an invariant and want a fail-fast crash.

lateinit is useful for properties initialized after constructor, mostly in tests or Android framework classes. lazy initializes a value on first access.

Common mistakes#

  • Using lateinit to avoid proper constructor injection.
  • Using !! instead of modeling nullable state.
  • Exposing nullable values where sealed UI state would be clearer.

Data classes and sealed classes/interfaces#

Data classes are useful for immutable values and UI state. Sealed classes/interfaces model a closed hierarchy of states or events.

sealed interface PaymentState {
    data object Idle : PaymentState
    data object Loading : PaymentState
    data class Requires3ds(val url: String) : PaymentState
    data class Failed(val message: String) : PaymentState
    data object Success : PaymentState
}

Interview wording#

“I use sealed hierarchies when the set of states is known and I want exhaustive when. It helps avoid boolean soup such as isLoading, isError, isEmpty, isSuccess conflicting with each other.”

Inline, reified, higher-order functions, and extensions#

Higher-order functions allow behavior to be passed as values. Inline can reduce allocation overhead for small lambdas and enables reified type parameters.

inline fun <reified T> Json.decodeOrNull(json: String): T? =
    runCatching { decodeFromString<T>(json) }.getOrNull()

Extensions improve readability but should not hide complex behavior or create surprising APIs.

Generics and variance#

out means producer covariance; in means consumer contravariance. This is common in repositories, mappers, result wrappers, and UI abstractions.

interface Mapper<in From, out To> {
    fun map(value: From): To
}
Coroutines and Concurrencyexpand / collapse

Structured concurrency#

Simple explanation#

Structured concurrency means coroutines have clear parent-child relationships. When the parent is cancelled, children are cancelled. When a child fails, the parent is notified according to the scope semantics.

Senior-level explanation#

Structured concurrency gives lifecycle ownership to asynchronous work. In Android, this prevents work from outliving screens or feature scopes. It also makes failures and cancellation predictable. Unstructured work such as GlobalScope.launch is dangerous because no component owns it.

class RefreshOrdersUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val api: OrdersApi,
    private val dao: OrdersDao,
    private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke() = withContext(dispatcher) {
        val remote = api.getOrders()
        dao.replaceAll(remote.map { it.toEntity() })
    }
}

Common mistakes#

  • Using GlobalScope for app work.
  • Launching child coroutines without waiting for them.
  • Swallowing cancellation.
  • Creating custom scopes without clear lifecycle.

Interview wording#

“I design coroutine ownership explicitly. UI work belongs to viewModelScope or lifecycle scopes; domain suspend functions do not launch unowned background work. If a parent operation is cancelled, its children should normally be cancelled too.”

launch vs async#

launch returns Job and is used for fire-and-observe work. async returns Deferred<T> and is used when you need a result, especially for parallel decomposition.

suspend fun loadHome(): HomeData = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { profileRepository.getProfile() }
    val feed = async { feedRepository.getFeed() }
    HomeData(profile.await(), feed.await())
}

Senior note#

Do not use async just because you want concurrency. If the result is not awaited, exceptions can be delayed or lost depending on context. Use async when the result is part of the parent operation.

coroutineScope vs supervisorScope#

coroutineScope fails fast: if one child fails, the scope cancels other children and rethrows the exception. This is correct when all children are part of one atomic operation.

supervisorScope isolates child failures: one child failure does not cancel siblings. This is useful when partial success is acceptable.

suspend fun loadDashboard(): Dashboard = supervisorScope {
    val recommendations = async { runCatching { recsRepository.load() } }
    val banners = async { runCatching { bannersRepository.load() } }

    Dashboard(
        recommendations = recommendations.await().getOrDefault(emptyList()),
        banners = banners.await().getOrDefault(emptyList())
    )
}

Interview wording#

“I choose coroutineScope when the operation is all-or-nothing. I choose supervisorScope when independent children can fail without invalidating the whole screen.”

Cancellation#

Cancellation is cooperative. Suspending functions check cancellation automatically, but CPU loops must check it manually using ensureActive() or isActive.

suspend fun parseLargeFile(lines: Sequence<String>): List<Item> = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    lines.mapIndexed { index, line ->
        ensureActive()
        parseLine(index, line)
    }.toList()
}

Common mistakes#

  • Catching Exception and swallowing CancellationException.
  • Doing blocking IO on Main dispatcher.
  • Not cancelling work when UI leaves screen.
try {
    repository.refresh()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: Throwable) {
    handleError(e)
}

Exception handling#

Exceptions in coroutines depend on builder and parent scope. launch propagates failure to parent immediately. async stores failure and rethrows on await. CoroutineExceptionHandler is not a local try/catch replacement; it catches uncaught exceptions at the boundary.

Interview wording#

“I prefer local error modeling in suspend functions and ViewModels. I do not rely on CoroutineExceptionHandler for normal business errors. I use it only as a last-resort boundary for uncaught failures.”

Dispatchers and withContext#

Use Main for UI, IO for blocking IO, Default for CPU-bound work. withContext changes dispatcher while preserving structured concurrency.

suspend fun loadUser(): User = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    api.getUser().toDomain()
}

In tests, inject dispatchers instead of hardcoding them.

Flowexpand / collapse

Cold Flow vs Hot Flow#

Cold Flow starts executing when collected. Each collector triggers the upstream again. Hot Flow exists independently of collectors and can emit even when nobody is collecting.

Room queries are often cold flows. StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot.

Interview wording#

“Cold Flow describes a stream pipeline; hot Flow represents shared state or events. I choose based on ownership: who produces the data and whether the stream should exist without collectors.”

StateFlow vs SharedFlow vs Channel#

StateFlow represents state. It always has a current value and replays the latest value to new collectors. It is ideal for UI state.

SharedFlow represents shared events or broadcasts. It is configurable with replay and buffer.

Channel is a communication primitive for point-to-point events. For UI one-shot events, many teams use SharedFlow with replay = 0, or model events as part of state if delivery guarantees are important.

data class LoginUiState(
    val email: String = "",
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null
)

sealed interface LoginEvent {
    data object NavigateHome : LoginEvent
}

private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(LoginUiState())
val uiState = _uiState.asStateFlow()

private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<LoginEvent>()
val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

Common mistakes#

  • Using StateFlow for one-time navigation without clearing consumed state.
  • Using SharedFlow for screen state and losing current value.
  • Not collecting with lifecycle awareness.

collect vs collectLatest#

collect processes every value. collectLatest cancels the previous block when a new value arrives. Use collectLatest for search results, image loading, or UI rendering where only the latest value matters.

combine, flatMapLatest, debounce, catch, retry#

combine merges latest values from multiple flows. flatMapLatest switches to a new inner flow and cancels the old one. debounce delays emissions until input stabilizes. catch handles upstream errors. retry retries upstream on failure.

val results: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = query
    .debounce(300)
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { q -> repository.search(q) }
    .map { SearchUiState.Content(it) }
    .catch { emit(SearchUiState.Error) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState.Idle)

Testing Flow#

Use Turbine for deterministic Flow assertions and runTest for virtual time.

@Test
fun `emits loading then content`() = runTest {
    viewModel.uiState.test {
        assertEquals(UiState.Loading, awaitItem())
        assertEquals(UiState.Content(items), awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}
Jetpack Composeexpand / collapse

Recomposition#

Simple explanation#

Recomposition means Compose re-executes composable functions when observed state changes. It does not redraw the whole screen blindly; Compose tries to update only what changed.

Senior-level explanation#

Composable functions should be side-effect free. Recomposition can happen often and for reasons you do not fully control. Expensive work should not be performed directly in the composable body. State should be stable and hoisted where appropriate.

@Composable
fun ProductScreen(
    viewModel: ProductViewModel = hiltViewModel(),
    onBack: () -> Unit
) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    ProductContent(
        state = state,
        onAction = viewModel::onAction,
        onBack = onBack
    )
}

remember and rememberSaveable#

remember survives recomposition but not Activity recreation. rememberSaveable survives configuration changes using a saved-state mechanism for saveable values.

State hoisting#

State hoisting means moving state up to the caller and making composables stateless where possible.

@Composable
fun SearchBar(
    query: String,
    onQueryChange: (String) -> Unit
) {
    TextField(value = query, onValueChange = onQueryChange)
}

Interview wording#

“I hoist state when the parent needs to control it, when it must be shared, or when I want testable stateless UI. I keep local state only when it is purely internal UI behavior.”

Compose side effects#

Use side-effect APIs to connect declarative UI with imperative world:

  • LaunchedEffect for suspend work tied to composition key;
  • DisposableEffect for setup/cleanup;
  • SideEffect for publishing successful composition state;
  • rememberCoroutineScope for user-triggered coroutines;
  • snapshotFlow for converting Compose state reads into Flow.

Common mistakes#

  • Starting coroutines directly in composable body.
  • Using unstable keys for LaunchedEffect.
  • Collecting events without lifecycle awareness.

Compose performance#

Use stable state models, avoid unnecessary allocations in composables, provide keys in lazy lists, avoid heavy computation in composition, and measure before optimizing.

LazyColumn {
    items(
        items = state.products,
        key = { it.id }
    ) { product ->
        ProductRow(product = product)
    }
}
Architectureexpand / collapse

MVVM and MVI#

MVVM separates UI from state and behavior. ViewModel exposes observable UI state and handles user actions. MVI emphasizes unidirectional data flow: actions/events go in, state comes out.

A senior answer should not sell one pattern as universally best. The right choice depends on team size, complexity, testing needs, and consistency.

Clean Architecture#

Clean Architecture separates concerns into layers: presentation, domain, and data. Dependencies should point inward. Domain should not depend on Android framework.

Senior-level trade-off#

Clean Architecture improves testability and boundaries, but overusing use cases and abstractions can create boilerplate. For simple features, a pragmatic repository + ViewModel may be enough. For complex business rules, use cases and domain models become valuable.

class PlaceOrderUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val cartRepository: CartRepository,
    private val paymentRepository: PaymentRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(request: PlaceOrderRequest): PlaceOrderResult {
        val cart = cartRepository.getCart()
        require(cart.items.isNotEmpty())
        return paymentRepository.placeOrder(cart, request.paymentMethod)
    }
}

Repository pattern and source of truth#

Repository hides data source details and exposes domain-friendly APIs. In offline-first apps, local database is usually the source of truth; network updates the database, and UI observes local data.

fun observeProducts(): Flow<List<Product>> =
    productDao.observeAll().map { entities -> entities.map { it.toDomain() } }

suspend fun refreshProducts() {
    val remote = api.getProducts()
    productDao.replaceAll(remote.map { it.toEntity() })
}

UI state modeling#

Avoid many unrelated mutable flags. Prefer a clear UI state model with loading, content, empty, and error states. For complex screens, combine stable data classes with sealed states.

Modularization#

Modularization improves build times, ownership, boundaries, and parallel development. It also increases Gradle complexity and requires clear dependency rules.

Interview wording#

“I modularize when there is a real scaling problem: build time, team ownership, feature isolation, or dependency boundaries. I avoid creating modules only for architectural aesthetics.”

Dependency Injectionexpand / collapse

Manual DI, Service Locator, Dagger, and Hilt#

DI means dependencies are provided from outside instead of being created internally. Constructor injection is preferred because it makes dependencies explicit and testable.

Hilt reduces boilerplate around Dagger and integrates with Android lifecycles.

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {
    @Provides
    @Singleton
    fun provideOkHttpClient(): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder().build()
}

Scopes#

Scopes define dependency lifetime. @Singleton lives for the application. @ActivityScoped lives for Activity component. @ViewModelScoped lives for ViewModel component.

Common mistakes#

  • Injecting Activity context into singleton.
  • Misunderstanding scope as thread-safety guarantee.
  • Adding scopes everywhere without lifetime reasoning.
  • Using field injection in places where constructor injection is possible.

Testing with DI#

In tests, replace real dependencies with fakes. Prefer fakes for behavior and mocks for interaction verification when necessary.

Networkingexpand / collapse

Retrofit and OkHttp#

Retrofit maps HTTP APIs to Kotlin interfaces. OkHttp handles low-level HTTP, connection pooling, interceptors, and caching.

Interceptors and token refresh#

Use application interceptors for adding headers and logging. Token refresh must avoid infinite loops and concurrent refresh storms.

Production design#

  • Attach access token to requests.
  • On 401, synchronize refresh.
  • Retry the original request once with the new token.
  • If refresh fails, clear session and emit logout/session-expired event.

Error handling#

Map transport errors, HTTP errors, serialization errors, and business errors separately. Do not leak Retrofit/OkHttp exceptions directly into UI.

sealed interface NetworkError {
    data object NoConnection : NetworkError
    data object Unauthorized : NetworkError
    data class Server(val code: Int) : NetworkError
    data object Unknown : NetworkError
}

Pagination, caching, and retry#

Pagination requires stable keys, duplicate handling, loading states, and error recovery. Retry should be explicit and limited; not every request should retry automatically.

Persistenceexpand / collapse

Room and SQLite#

Room is an abstraction over SQLite with compile-time query validation. Use transactions for multi-step updates that must be atomic.

@Dao
interface ProductDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY name")
    fun observeProducts(): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>

    @Transaction
    suspend fun replaceAll(items: List<ProductEntity>) {
        clear()
        insertAll(items)
    }
}

DataStore vs SharedPreferences#

DataStore is the modern choice for asynchronous, transactional key-value or typed preferences. SharedPreferences is legacy and synchronous by default.

Use DataStore for preferences, feature flags, onboarding state, and small settings. Do not use it as a relational database.

Migrations#

Database migrations must be tested. A broken migration is a production data-loss bug, not just a local crash.

Testingexpand / collapse

Unit, integration, and UI tests#

Unit tests validate isolated logic. Integration tests validate collaboration between components. UI tests validate user-visible behavior. A senior test strategy chooses the cheapest test that gives enough confidence.

ViewModel tests#

ViewModel tests should control dispatchers, use fake repositories, and assert state/events.

@Test
fun `login success emits navigation event`() = runTest {
    val repository = FakeAuthRepository(success = true)
    val viewModel = LoginViewModel(repository, testDispatcher)

    viewModel.events.test {
        viewModel.onAction(LoginAction.Submit)
        assertEquals(LoginEvent.NavigateHome, awaitItem())
    }
}

Fake vs mock#

Use fakes when you want realistic behavior and state. Use mocks when you need to verify a specific interaction. Over-mocking makes tests brittle.

Coroutine and Flow testing#

Use runTest, injected dispatchers, virtual time, and Turbine. Avoid real delays and real dispatchers in unit tests.

Performanceexpand / collapse

Memory leaks#

Leaks happen when long-lived objects keep references to short-lived objects. Common Android leaks include Activity context in singletons, Fragment binding after onDestroyView, callbacks not unregistered, and coroutines outliving lifecycle.

ANR and threading#

ANR happens when the main thread is blocked. Avoid disk, network, heavy JSON parsing, bitmap decoding, or long computations on Main.

Startup performance#

Startup is affected by Application initialization, DI graph creation, synchronous disk IO, content providers, and heavy first-screen work. Lazy initialization and baseline profiles can help, but measure first.

Rendering and Compose performance#

Jank appears when frames miss the rendering deadline. Avoid unnecessary recomposition, unstable list keys, heavy work in composables, and large images without optimization.

Profiling#

Use Android Studio Profiler, Layout Inspector, Macrobenchmark, Baseline Profiles, StrictMode, and logs/metrics. A senior answer should include how you would measure, not only how you would guess.

Android System Designexpand / collapse

Designing a chat app#

Cover authentication, local database as source of truth, WebSocket or push for real-time updates, message queue for offline sends, delivery/read state, pagination, conflict handling, media uploads, encryption/security if needed, and observability.

Designing an offline-first app#

Use local database as source of truth, sync workers, conflict resolution, retry/backoff, network constraints, and clear UI states for stale/syncing/error.

Designing a payment flow#

Payment requires idempotency, secure token handling, backend-driven state, 3DS handling, error recovery, analytics, and strong testing. Do not trust client-only success state.

Designing a news feed#

Discuss pagination, caching, pull-to-refresh, local source of truth, deduplication, prefetching, image loading, offline state, and experimentation/analytics.

Designing navigation architecture#

Navigation should be explicit, testable, and feature-aware. Avoid passing large objects through navigation arguments. Model deep links, back stack behavior, and one-shot navigation events carefully.

Senior Deep Dive + Follow-up Answersexpand / collapse

What was expanded

This block adds the missing Senior-level layer: answers to follow-up questions, production trade-offs, common mistakes, and interview-ready wording. The goal is not to memorize APIs, but to explain ownership, lifecycle, failure semantics, testability, scalability, and observability.

Direct answers to follow-up questions from the main guide

Lifecycle

onPause vs onStop?
onPause means the Activity is losing foreground focus and can still be visible. onStop means it is no longer visible. Avoid heavy synchronous work in onPause.

Is onDestroy always called?
No. System process death may skip it, so critical persistence must not depend on onDestroy.

Why viewLifecycleOwner in Fragment?
Fragment instance can outlive its View. View-bound collectors/listeners must use the view lifecycle to avoid leaks.

When is Application context not enough?
For UI-bound operations requiring an Activity theme, window token, dialog, or activity result.

Coroutines

Why is GlobalScope dangerous?
It creates work without a structured owner. The job may outlive the screen or feature that started it.

What happens when the parent is cancelled?
Children are cancelled too. Cancellation is cooperative, so blocking code may delay it.

launch exception vs async exception?
launch propagates uncaught exceptions through the parent/root handler. async stores the exception and rethrows it at await(), but child failure can still affect the parent.

Does supervisorScope handle errors automatically?
No. It isolates sibling cancellation, but you still need explicit error handling.

Dispatchers.IO vs Default?
IO is for blocking IO. Default is for CPU-bound work.

When use NonCancellable?
Only for short critical cleanup in finally, not to ignore cancellation for normal work.

Flow

stateIn vs shareIn?
stateIn creates a StateFlow with an initial/current value. shareIn creates a configurable SharedFlow.

What does replay = 0 mean?
New collectors do not receive previous emissions. This is unsafe for state or critical events.

Can Channel be used for UI events?
Sometimes, but it is not the default. First decide whether the event is actually state.

Compose

Why must composables be side-effect free?
They can be recomposed multiple times. Direct side effects may repeat navigation, analytics, or snackbars.

When use rememberUpdatedState?
When a long-lived effect must use the latest callback/value without restarting.

rememberCoroutineScope vs LaunchedEffect?
LaunchedEffect reacts to entering composition/key changes. rememberCoroutineScope is for launching work from event handlers.

Why LazyColumn keys?
Keys preserve item identity and remembered state across insert/remove/reorder.

Architecture and system design

Is domain layer always needed?
No. Add it when business logic is complex or reused; otherwise it can be ceremony.

DTO vs domain model?
DTO is a transport/storage contract. Domain model represents business meaning. UI model represents presentation needs.

How avoid duplicate chat messages after reconnect?
Use client ids, server ids, idempotency, local pending/sent/failed state, and deterministic merge logic.

How design failed message retry?
Keep the failed message locally with a retry action and reuse the same idempotency key.

1. Lifecycle, configuration changes, and process death

Senior-level explanation

Do not explain Activity/Fragment lifecycle as a callback list. Explain state ownership. A ViewModel survives configuration changes, but not system-initiated process death. SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable are for small recoverable UI state, not for storing full screen models.

State type Owner Example
Ephemeral UI state remember dropdown expanded state
Recoverable UI element state rememberSaveable, SavedStateHandle selected tab, query text
Screen state ViewModel loading/content/error
Durable data Repository + DB/DataStore session, cached feed, pending writes 
@HiltViewModel
class ProductDetailsViewModel @Inject constructor(
    savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repository: ProductsRepository
) : ViewModel() {
    private val productId = savedStateHandle.getStateFlow("productId", "")

    val uiState = productId
        .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
        .flatMapLatest(repository::observeProduct)
        .map<Product, ProductDetailsUiState> { ProductDetailsUiState.Content(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProductDetailsUiState.Loading)
}

Follow-up answers

How is rememberSaveable different from SavedStateHandle?
rememberSaveable is local Compose UI-element state. SavedStateHandle belongs to the ViewModel and is appropriate when the value affects screen logic or repository queries.

When is ViewModel overkill?
When the state is purely local and short-lived: animation state, a temporary expanded card, drag state, or local focus state.

What should not go into a Bundle/SavedStateHandle?
Large lists, bitmaps, DTO graphs, full API responses, or sensitive data. Store minimal keys and rebuild state from the data layer.

Why clear Fragment binding in onDestroyView()?
The Fragment instance can outlive its View hierarchy. Keeping binding after onDestroyView() leaks views, Context, listeners, and adapters.

2. Background work: Services, BroadcastReceiver, WorkManager

Senior-level explanation

Choose APIs based on task semantics:

Task semantics Preferred tool
Screen-bound short work viewModelScope / lifecycleScope
Deferrable guaranteed work WorkManager
User-visible long-running work Foreground Service
Real-time stream for one screen lifecycle-aware owner
System event Receiver, with restrictions in mind 
class SyncOrdersWorker(
    appContext: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters,
    private val repository: OrdersRepository
) : CoroutineWorker(appContext, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = try {
        repository.syncPendingOrders()
        Result.success()
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        if (runAttemptCount < 3) Result.retry() else Result.failure()
    }
}

Follow-up answers

Why is IntentService no longer a good default?
Modern Android background limits make service-first designs fragile. Deferrable guaranteed work belongs to WorkManager.

When is a foreground service justified?
Only for genuinely user-visible long-running operations such as navigation, active tracking, recording, or explicit upload/download.

What is unique work?
Named WorkManager work with a conflict policy. It prevents multiple duplicated sync jobs after repeated user actions or app events.

How do you debug WorkManager?
Log work id, name, constraints, attempt count, result, payload size, and failure reason. Use the inspector locally and production metrics for sync health.

3. Kotlin as state modeling, not trivia

Senior-level explanation

Kotlin interview questions should be connected to real Android design. sealed interface, immutable data class, null-safety, constructor injection, and extension functions are useful when they reduce invalid states and improve readability.

sealed interface CheckoutUiState {
    data object Loading : CheckoutUiState
    data class Content(
        val cart: Cart,
        val paymentMethods: List<PaymentMethod>
    ) : CheckoutUiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : CheckoutUiState
}

Follow-up answers

When is sealed interface better than enum?
When each state can carry different data. Enum is better for simple fixed values without payload.

When is lateinit appropriate?
Mostly when framework construction prevents constructor injection. Otherwise, prefer constructor injection or explicit initialization.

When is an extension function a smell?
When it hides dependencies, IO, navigation, analytics, or complex business logic. Extensions are best for small pure transformations.

Why does immutability matter for Compose?
Immutable snapshots make state transitions predictable, easier to test, and easier for Compose to reason about.

4. Coroutines: structured concurrency, cancellation, exceptions

Senior-level explanation

A Senior coroutine answer should always cover three questions: who owns the work, who cancels it, and how failures propagate.

suspend fun loadCheckoutScreen(
    cartRepository: CartRepository,
    paymentRepository: PaymentRepository
): CheckoutData = coroutineScope {
    val cart = async { cartRepository.getCart() }
    val methods = async { paymentRepository.getPaymentMethods() }
    CheckoutData(cart.await(), methods.await())
}

Use coroutineScope when child tasks are one all-or-nothing operation. Use supervisorScope when children can fail independently.

Follow-up answers

Why is GlobalScope a bad default?
It has no structured parent and can outlive the screen, ViewModel, or feature that started the work.

When is an application-wide scope acceptable?
For explicitly designed app-level work such as analytics queues, session observers, or shared socket managers. It should be injected, observable, and cancellable when appropriate.

Where does an exception from async appear?
At await(), but that does not mean it is isolated. In a regular parent scope, child failure can still cancel the parent and siblings.

Why is CancellationException not a user error?
Cancellation is a normal control path: screen closed, query changed, job replaced. Do not convert it to “Something went wrong”.

When use SupervisorJob instead of supervisorScope?
supervisorScope is local to a suspend operation. SupervisorJob defines the failure behavior of a longer-lived scope.

What about CoroutineExceptionHandler?
It is not a universal try/catch. It handles uncaught exceptions in root coroutines; async still requires handling around await().

5. Flow: cold/hot, StateFlow, SharedFlow, Channel, events

Senior-level explanation

Explain Flow through delivery semantics.

API Semantics Android use case
Flow cold stream repository query, Room observable
StateFlow hot state holder with current value screen state
SharedFlow configurable hot broadcast shared signals
Channel queue / point-to-point internal command processing 
val uiState: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = query
    .debounce(300)
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { q -> repository.search(q) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SearchUiState.Empty)

Follow-up answers

Why is Flow cold by default?
Each collector starts the upstream again. If upstream performs a network call, multiple collectors can trigger multiple calls.

stateIn vs shareIn?
stateIn creates StateFlow with initial/current value. shareIn creates SharedFlow with configurable replay and buffer.

What does WhileSubscribed(5_000) do?
It keeps upstream alive briefly after subscribers disappear, which avoids unnecessary restarts during configuration changes.

When is Channel justified?
For queue-like or actor-like internal processing, not as a default UI event mechanism.

How model one-shot navigation?
First check whether it is actually state. For example, login success can be isLoggedIn = true, and the UI performs navigation from a LaunchedEffect.

Why can collectLatest be dangerous?
It cancels the previous block. Good for search, bad for non-interruptible work such as payments, writes, or analytics.

6. Compose: recomposition, state hoisting, side effects, performance

Senior-level explanation

Composable functions must be idempotent and side-effect free. Navigation, snackbar, analytics, listeners, and coroutines should go through effect APIs with correct keys.

@Composable
fun CheckoutRoute(
    viewModel: CheckoutViewModel,
    snackbarHostState: SnackbarHostState,
    onPaymentSuccess: () -> Unit
) {
    val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    val latestSuccess by rememberUpdatedState(onPaymentSuccess)

    LaunchedEffect(uiState.paymentCompleted) {
        if (uiState.paymentCompleted) latestSuccess()
    }

    LaunchedEffect(uiState.errorMessage) {
        uiState.errorMessage?.let { snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(it) }
    }
}

Follow-up answers

Why is recomposition not a full redraw?
Compose reruns only the relevant parts of the composition that depend on changed state and can skip stable unchanged parts.

Why not run side effects directly in a composable body?
The body can execute many times. Direct calls can duplicate navigation, analytics, or snackbar events.

remember vs rememberSaveable?
remember survives recomposition. rememberSaveable also survives recreation for saveable UI element state.

Where should state live: UI or ViewModel?
Local interaction state in UI; business/screen state in ViewModel. The right owner is more important than dogma.

Why use rememberUpdatedState?
To keep a long-lived effect using the latest lambda/value without restarting the effect.

When use DisposableEffect?
For setup/cleanup: lifecycle observers, listeners, sensors, receivers.

When is derivedStateOf useful?
When inputs change frequently but the derived output changes less often.

Why LazyColumn keys?
They preserve item identity, remembered state, and reduce incorrect state reuse after insert/remove/reorder.

7. Architecture, Clean Architecture, modularization

Senior-level explanation

Describe architecture through boundaries and data flow, not labels.

UI renders immutable state and sends actions. ViewModel is the screen state holder. Repository hides data sources and acts as a single source of truth. Use cases are added when complexity or reuse justifies them. Modules exist for ownership, visibility, testability, and build isolation.

Follow-up answers

When is a domain layer unnecessary?
When a use case only forwards one repository call and adds no policy, orchestration, validation, or reuse.

MVVM vs MVI practically?
MVVM separates UI and state holder. MVI enforces stricter unidirectional state transitions. In production, discipline matters more than labels.

How avoid DTO leaking into UI?
Map DTOs to domain/UI models at boundaries. DTOs represent transport contracts, not presentation needs.

How choose module boundaries?
By ownership, dependency direction, and change frequency, not by folder aesthetics.

When does modularization hurt?
When modules are too granular, dependency setup becomes noisy, or navigation/testing complexity grows without ownership/build benefits.

8. Hilt and DI scopes

Follow-up answers

When is @ActivityRetainedScoped better than @ViewModelScoped?
When one instance must be shared by multiple ViewModels and survive configuration changes.

Why can too many singletons be harmful?
They can hold stale state, leak Context, hide mutable global state, and make tests harder.

Constructor injection vs module provider?
Constructor injection is the default for your own classes. Providers are for third-party/framework types or interface bindings.

How replace dependencies in tests?
Use graph replacement with Hilt test modules/fakes instead of monkey-patching global singletons.

9. Testing coroutines, Flow, ViewModel

Senior-level explanation

Design async code to be testable: inject dispatchers, use fake repositories, control Flow producers, and avoid real time.

@Test
fun emitsLoadingThenContent() = runTest {
    val repository = FakeArticlesRepository()
    val viewModel = FeedViewModel(repository)

    viewModel.uiState.test {
        assertEquals(FeedUiState.Loading, awaitItem())
        repository.emitArticles(listOf(Article("1", "Coroutines")))
        assertTrue(awaitItem() is FeedUiState.Content)
    }
}

Follow-up answers

Fake vs mock?
Use fakes for stateful async behavior. Use mocks when interaction verification is the actual contract.

StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher?
Standard gives explicit scheduling control. Unconfined is simpler but can hide scheduling issues.

Why one shared scheduler?
Virtual time must be consistent across all test dispatchers, otherwise advanceUntilIdle() may not flush everything.

Why not runBlocking?
It blocks real threads and lacks virtual time control. runTest is built for coroutine tests.

How test infinite flows?
Collect in backgroundScope, use Turbine, and cancel collection explicitly.

10. Performance, leaks, ANR, system design

Follow-up answers

How explain a memory leak?
An object is no longer needed but remains reachable from GC roots. In Android, common causes are static references, listeners, adapters, binding leaks, callbacks, and long-lived coroutines.

How find the leak?
Inspect the reference chain from GC root using LeakCanary or Memory Profiler, then remove or shorten the owning reference.

What causes ANR?
Main-thread blocking: slow IO, locks, heavy inflation, binder calls, synchronous DB work, or long receiver/service operations.

How optimize startup?
Measure cold/warm/hot startup, remove eager initialization from Application.onCreate, lazy-load non-critical work, optimize DI/content providers, and add Baseline Profiles for critical paths.

How answer Android system design questions?
Start with invariants: source of truth, read path, write path, offline behavior, sync/retry, lifecycle owner, error handling, testing, observability.

How avoid duplicate chat messages after reconnect?
Use client-generated ids, server ids, pending/sent/failed states, idempotent sends, and local DB deduplication.

How design token refresh?
Single-flight refresh using mutex/synchronization, retry original request once, clear session on unrecoverable refresh failure, and keep token logic out of UI.

Who initiates navigation?
UI owns the actual NavController. ViewModel exposes state or result; UI performs navigation as a side effect.

Interview-ready summary

Coroutines: define owner, cancellation, and failure semantics before choosing API.
Flow: distinguish state from delivery and cold from hot.
Compose: keep composables side-effect free and choose correct state owner.
Architecture: talk in boundaries, source of truth, and trade-offs.
Testing: make async behavior deterministic by design.
Performance: measure first, then apply targeted fixes.

Senior Edge Cases: a bank of production trapsexpand / collapse

This section is a concentrate of the traps that separate Senior from Middle. Each case follows the same scheme: problem → why it happens → what breaks in production → what a Senior does. In interviews these stories are the most convincing material, because they cannot be memorized from docs — only earned in production.

1. Token refresh: several 401s at once#

Problem. The access token expires and 5 parallel requests receive 401 at the same time. A naive implementation fires 5 refresh calls.

Why. OkHttp invokes the Authenticator for every failed response independently. Without synchronization, every thread believes it is the one that must refresh.

Production impact. If the backend rotates refresh tokens (one-time use), the first refresh invalidates the refresh token and the remaining four get 401 on the refresh endpoint — and the usual "401 on refresh = log the user out" logic mass-evicts users. The classic incident: a logout spike after a release with no visible cause.

Senior approach. Serialize refresh behind a Mutex: the first thread refreshes, the rest wait, and after entering the critical section re-check whether someone already refreshed. Plus a retry cap to avoid loops.

class TokenAuthenticator @Inject constructor(
    private val tokenStore: TokenStore,
    private val refreshApi: RefreshApi
) : Authenticator {
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    override fun authenticate(route: Route?, response: Response): Request? {
        if (response.priorCount() >= 2) return null // loop guard
        val failedToken = response.request.header("Authorization")
            ?.removePrefix("Bearer ")

        val newToken = runBlocking {
            mutex.withLock {
                val current = tokenStore.accessToken()
                // Someone refreshed while we were waiting on the mutex
                if (current != null && current != failedToken) current
                else refreshApi.refresh(tokenStore.refreshToken())
                    ?.also { tokenStore.save(it) }
            }
        } ?: return null // refresh failed -> logout flow

        return response.request.newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken")
            .build()
    }

    private fun Response.priorCount(): Int =
        generateSequence(priorResponse) { it.priorResponse }.count()
}

A common follow-up: why an Authenticator and not an interceptor? Because the Authenticator is invoked only on 401 and already holds the failed response, while an interceptor would have to distinguish statuses and replay requests manually. The interceptor remains responsible for proactively attaching the current token to every request.

2. Flow: catch only handles upstream#

Problem. A developer adds .catch { } and assumes the Flow is now "safe". The crash still happens.

Why. catch intercepts exceptions only from operators above it in the chain (exception transparency). An exception inside collect { } is downstream — it flies past catch and crashes the collector's scope.

Production impact. A crash in render logic (say, NumberFormatException while formatting backend data) kills the coroutine and with it the state subscription. The UI "freezes": state keeps updating but nobody collects anymore.

Senior approach. Keep collect razor-thin (assignment/rendering of a ready model only), move mapping and validation upstream (map/mapNotNull), and model errors as part of UI state rather than as exceptions.

repository.orders()
    .map { it.toUiModel() }          // a failure here -> catch works
    .catch { emit(OrdersUi.Error(it)) }
    .collect { ui ->
        _state.value = ui            // assignment only, nothing to fail
    }

3. StateFlow: equal values never reach collectors#

Problem. The ViewModel emits a "new" state but the UI does not update. Or fast intermediate values are lost.

Why. StateFlow (1) conflates — a slow collector only sees the latest value; (2) compares the new value to the old via equals() and skips emission when they are equal. For a data class with identical fields, copy() produces an equal object — no emission.

Production impact. The typical case is "re-showing" a one-shot event via state: state.copy(showToast = true) does nothing the second time because the value is already true and equal. Or an error snackbar fails to appear for the second identical error.

Senior approach. Separate state and events: state lives in StateFlow (where conflation and deduplication are desirable), one-shot events go through a dedicated effects channel (Channel.receiveAsFlow() or a carefully configured SharedFlow). If "equal" emissions are genuinely semantically distinct, add a discriminator field (timestamp/id) — but that is usually a smell that an event was stuffed into state.

4. SharedFlow: replay, buffer and dropped events#

Problem. An event emitted into a SharedFlow(replay = 0) before any subscriber exists disappears forever. Or tryEmit silently returns false and the event is lost.

Why. A SharedFlow without replay keeps no history; emit with BufferOverflow.SUSPEND and zero buffer suspends until all subscribers accept the value, and in that configuration tryEmit simply fails when a slow subscriber exists.

Production impact. A navigation event sent during Activity recreation (no subscriber for a moment) is dropped — the user taps a button and nothing happens. Nearly impossible to reproduce locally.

Senior approach. For one-shot events use Channel(BUFFERED) + receiveAsFlow(): the channel holds events until a consumer appears and guarantees delivery to exactly one consumer. State the trade-off explicitly: a Channel does not support multiple subscribers, but for navigation/toasts that is precisely the semantics you want.

5. Compose: unstable parameters and excessive recomposition#

Problem. The list stutters; the profiler shows hundreds of recompositions in composables whose data "did not change".

Why. Compose can skip recomposition only when all parameters are stable and equal to the previous ones. List, classes with var, types from modules without compiler metadata are unstable — Compose plays safe and always recomposes. A separate trap: lambdas capturing an unstable object.

Production impact. Scroll jank and extra battery drain on mid-range devices; invisible on the developers' flagship phones.

Senior approach. Read compiler metrics and Layout Inspector recomposition counts instead of guessing. Make UI models immutable (val + kotlinx.collections.immutable, or @Immutable/@Stable with the contract actually honored), hoist lambdas into remember or method references, use a stability configuration file for classes from other modules. And always add: measure first — not every recomposition is a problem.

@Immutable
data class CartItemUi(
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val priceFormatted: String
)

@Composable
fun CartRow(item: CartItemUi, onClick: (String) -> Unit) { /* ... */ }
// Call site: onClick = remember { { id -> viewModel.onItemClick(id) } }
// or a method reference: viewModel::onItemClick

6. Fragment: lifecycleScope vs viewLifecycleOwner#

Problem. Collecting in fragment.lifecycleScope updates a view that no longer exists, or subscriptions get duplicated.

Why. A Fragment has two lifecycles: the fragment itself and its view. On the back stack the view is destroyed (onDestroyView) while the fragment survives. A coroutine in lifecycleScope outlives the view and keeps references to destroyed binding/views. Returning from the back stack runs onViewCreated again — adding a second collector.

Production impact. View leaks, crashes on a null binding, doubled handlers (events delivered twice). The single most common Android leak in legacy codebases.

Senior approach. The canonical pattern: viewLifecycleOwner + repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED); binding nulled in onDestroyView. In code review this is the first thing checked in fragments.

override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            viewModel.state.collect(::render)
        }
    }
}

7. WorkManager: periodic work is not exact scheduling#

Problem. The business asks for "sync exactly every 15 minutes", the developer schedules PeriodicWorkRequest(15, MINUTES) — and sync runs "somewhere between 15 and 40 minutes, and not at all overnight".

Why. 15 minutes is the minimum interval, not a guarantee. The system batches work and defers it for Doze/App Standby buckets, constraints (network, battery) and vendor "optimizers" (some OEMs kill background work far more aggressively than AOSP).

Production impact. Data goes stale unpredictably; sync metrics look great in the office and terrible in the field. The team blames the backend for weeks.

Senior approach. State the rule: WorkManager is for deferrable guaranteed work. For exact timing — AlarmManager's setExactAndAllowWhileIdle (with the SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission and the awareness that Google restricts it to genuinely time-critical cases — alarms, reminders). For realtime — FCM push as a trigger. And always add sync-on-app-open as compensation: users see fresh data exactly when they look at the screen.

8. Room: destructive migration on user data#

Problem. A fallbackToDestructiveMigration() left over from prototyping ships to production. After a schema bump, part of the user base loses local data.

Why. It was convenient at MVP stage, and nobody wrote migration tests because "the schema will change anyway".

Production impact. For an offline-first app this is loss of unsynced user data: drafts, cart, local edits. That is not a bug — it is lost trust and a one-star review.

Senior approach. Enable exportSchema = true, keep schema JSONs in VCS, write explicit Migrations and test them with MigrationTestHelper against real schemas. A destructive fallback is acceptable only for a pure cache fully recoverable from the network — and that decision is recorded explicitly, not "left as is".

val MIGRATION_5_6 = object : Migration(5, 6) {
    override fun migrate(db: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        db.execSQL(
            "ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING'"
        )
        db.execSQL(
            "CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS index_orders_status ON orders(status)"
        )
    }
}

9. Paging 3: refresh, append and prepend are different errors#

Problem. Every paging error is rendered as a full-screen error. A user who scrolled deep into the list on a flaky network loses all already-loaded content from view.

Why. LoadState has three independent components — refresh, append, prepend — while the UI handles only one "generic" error.

Production impact. UX degrades exactly where Paging was supposed to help: on slow networks. Users report "the list disappears".

Senior approach. Map states separately: refresh.Error + empty cache → full-screen error with retry; refresh.Error + cached data → snackbar over content; append.Error → footer with a retry button; with a RemoteMediator, distinguish mediator.refresh from source.refresh (network failed, but the cache is still shown).

10. SavedStateHandle is not persistence#

Problem. Large objects or critical data get stuffed into SavedStateHandle "to survive process death".

Why. Three mechanisms with different guarantees get confused: SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable (survive recreation and process death, but small data only — the whole state goes through a Binder transaction with a ~1MB limit), in-memory ViewModel (survives only configuration change), persistent storage (survives everything including reboot).

Production impact. TransactionTooLargeException — a crash not in your code but when the system saves state; or a "lost" form because a ViewModel without SavedStateHandle did not survive a background kill.

Senior approach. A three-tier rule: identifiers and small UI state (scroll position, entered text, selected tab) → SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable; anything reloadable → reload by id; anything the user created and fears losing (a draft) → Room/DataStore at input time, not in onStop.

11. DataStore is not a database#

Problem. Entity lists, history, feed caches end up in Proto/Preferences DataStore — "because it is convenient, one Flow".

Why. DataStore reads and writes the whole file atomically. No partial updates, no queries, no indexes. Every change serializes the entire object.

Production impact. As the file grows, every write gets more expensive, updates contend (updateData is serialized), startup reads slow down. And partial data migration becomes impossible.

Senior approach. DataStore is for settings, tokens, flags, small config objects. Relational/list data belongs in Room. Additionally: always set a corruptionHandler (files do get corrupted) and use SharedPreferencesMigration when moving off legacy prefs.

val settingsStore: DataStore<Settings> = DataStoreFactory.create(
    serializer = SettingsSerializer,
    corruptionHandler = ReplaceFileCorruptionHandler { Settings.getDefaultInstance() },
    migrations = listOf(SharedPreferencesMigration(context, "legacy_prefs") { prefs, current ->
        current.toBuilder().setDarkTheme(prefs.getBoolean("dark", false)).build()
    })
) { context.dataStoreFile("settings.pb") }

12. R8: reflection, serialization and "works in debug, crashes in release"#

Problem. The release build crashes or silently returns null fields where debug works perfectly.

Why. R8 removes "unused" code and renames classes. Anything reached via reflection — Gson, Moshi in reflection mode, custom serialization, JNI, some DI patterns — breaks, because R8 cannot see those accesses. A separate trap: generic signatures that Gson reads from metadata vanish without -keepattributes Signature.

Production impact. The worst case is not a crash but silent nulls in DTOs: business logic runs on garbage data. Play Console crashes are unreadable without the mapping file.

Senior approach. (1) Remove reflection systematically: kotlinx.serialization or Moshi codegen instead of Gson — almost no keep rules needed. (2) Where reflection remains — targeted keep rules on the DTO package, never a global minification opt-out. (3) Test the release build (a smoke suite on the minified build in CI). (4) Upload mapping.txt to Play Console / Crashlytics and archive the mapping for every release.

// proguard-rules.pro (fragment, only if reflection-based serialization remains)
// -keepattributes Signature, *Annotation*
// -keep class com.app.network.dto.** { <fields>; }

13. PendingIntent: mutability as an attack vector#

Problem. A PendingIntent delegates your identity: the receiver executes the Intent on behalf of your app, with your permissions.

Why. A mutable PendingIntent wrapping an implicit intent lets a malicious app fill in the blanks (component, extras) and act in your name — a classic vulnerability. That is why targetSdk 31+ makes the mutability flag mandatory.

Production impact. Either a security hole (mutable where unnecessary), or an IllegalArgumentException crash when targeting a new SDK without an explicit flag, or broken notification actions when IMMUTABLE was set where the system must fill the Intent in (direct reply via RemoteInput requires MUTABLE).

Senior approach. Default — FLAG_IMMUTABLE + an explicit intent (component set). MUTABLE only for documented cases (RemoteInput, some bubbles/geofencing APIs), with the intent narrowed as much as possible. Knows FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT vs FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT semantics and that PendingIntents with the same request code/intent (per filterEquals) are the same system object.

val pi = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context,
    requestCode,
    Intent(context, OrderDetailsActivity::class.java)
        .putExtra("orderId", orderId),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
)

14. Deep links: an incoming URI is untrusted input#

Problem. Deep link parameters are consumed directly: a WebView opens a URL from a parameter, an id is plugged into a request, flags like isPremium=true influence logic.

Why. Anyone can craft a deep link: another app, a malicious site, an email. An exported Activity with an intent-filter is a public API of your app.

Production impact. Arbitrary URLs opened in a WebView carrying session cookies (phishing/token theft), paywall bypass via flags, crashes on garbage parameters, navigation into internal screens around authorization.

Senior approach. Validate every parameter (type, format, allow-list of hosts for URLs), never carry authorization decisions in a URI, gate deep links through the same auth-check layer as internal navigation. For trusted links — App Links with a verified domain (assetlinks.json) rather than a custom scheme any app can hijack. Enable StrictMode.detectUnsafeIntentLaunch in suspicious areas.

fun parseOrderDeepLink(uri: Uri): Screen? {
    val id = uri.getQueryParameter("orderId")
        ?.takeIf { it.matches(Regex("^[0-9]{1,12}$")) }
        ?: return null               // garbage -> home, no crash
    return Screen.OrderDetails(id)   // the navigation layer re-checks auth
}

15. Cancellation: swallowed CancellationException and NonCancellable cleanup#

Problem. A blanket catch (e: Exception) around suspend code also catches CancellationException — the coroutine "refuses to die" and scopes stop cancelling cleanly. The mirror problem: cleanup in finally calls a suspend function and is cut off immediately because the coroutine is already cancelled.

Why. Cancellation in coroutines is cooperative and implemented via an exception. It is a control signal, not an error.

Production impact. Work leaking past screen exit, zombie requests, unclosed resources, flaky tests. Very hard to debug because everything just "sometimes hangs".

Senior approach. Either catch specific exceptions or rethrow CancellationException; for suspend cleanup use withContext(NonCancellable) only for short critical operations (closing a transaction, finishing a log write).

try {
    syncOrders()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e                       // never swallow
} catch (e: IOException) {
    _state.value = SyncState.Error(e)
} finally {
    withContext(NonCancellable) { // otherwise a suspend call here dies instantly
        journal.write("sync finished")
    }
}

Follow-up questions by level#

Middle+: how do catch and retry differ in Flow?
Both operate only on upstream exceptions. retry re-subscribes to the upstream a given number of times (with a predicate and backoff via retryWhen); catch handles terminally: after it the upstream is complete, you can at most emit a fallback. Operator order is critical: retry before catch.

Senior: how do you test the "parallel 401s, single refresh" scenario?
MockWebServer: enqueue several 401s, one successful refresh and successful replays; launch N concurrent requests via async and assert exactly one request hit the refresh endpoint (counting recorded requests by path). A separate test: refresh returns 401 and all requests resolve into exactly one logout signal.

Staff/Lead: how do you scale this knowledge to the team instead of keeping it in one head?
Turn the cases into infrastructure: lint rules (ban fragment.lifecycleScope for collect, ban mutable PendingIntent without a justified suppress), shared base classes/conventions (a single TokenAuthenticator, a single LoadState mapper), CI gates (migration tests mandatory on schema change, smoke on the minified build), and ADRs explaining why. Knowledge not encoded into tooling leaves with people.

Android Platform Deep Dive: permissions, storage, notifications, startupexpand / collapse

Platform constraints are a favorite filter for candidates who only ever worked "inside the ViewModel". A Senior must know how Android's evolution broke and reshaped real apps.

Runtime permissions across Android versions#

  • Android 6 (API 23): dangerous permissions became runtime. The request → rationale → request pattern was born.
  • Android 10–11: background location split into a separate permission and flow; scoped storage became the default; one-time permissions ("Only this time"); auto-reset of permissions for unused apps.
  • Android 12: approximate vs precise location (the user may grant only coarse); new Bluetooth permissions (BLUETOOTH_SCAN/CONNECT) replacing location for BLE.
  • Android 13 (API 33): POST_NOTIFICATIONS — notifications are now opt-in; granular media permissions READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/VIDEO/AUDIO replacing READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.
  • Android 14 (API 34): partial photo access (READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED) — the user can grant access to selected photos only; mandatory foreground service types.

The Senior framing: "a permission is not a dialog, it is a state machine: granted / denied / permanently denied / partial — and it can change while the app is in background, which restarts the process". So permission state is checked at every use, never cached at startup.

Bonus points for saying the best permission is the one you never request: the Photo Picker provides photo selection with zero storage permissions, CREATE_DOCUMENT/SAF saves files without permissions — most media features need no media permission at all.

Scoped storage and file access#

The post-Android 10/11 model: an app freely owns only its app-specific directories (filesDir, getExternalFilesDir — no permissions, removed on uninstall). Shared media goes through MediaStore (your own inserts need no permission; reading others' media needs media permissions; editing others' media needs consent dialogs like createWriteRequest). Arbitrary documents — through the Storage Access Framework with persistable URI permissions. MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE is effectively banned by Play policy except for file managers.

Production trap: persistable URI permissions are limited in count and disappear on reinstall — document URIs stored in Room must be validated before use, or you get a SecurityException months after the user picked the file.

Notifications: channels, permission, FGS#

Channels (API 26+) are settings in the user's hands: importance, sound and vibration are set at channel creation and from then on owned by the user; you cannot programmatically raise importance. Channel design is therefore a product decision: separate channels for critical (order status) and marketing, so users can kill the latter without losing the former.

Android 13 adds POST_NOTIFICATIONS: the right strategy is to ask in a moment of value (after the first order: "want to track your delivery?"), not on first launch. Denial means a foreground service runs without a visible notification — alive, but invisible to the user.

Foreground services on Android 14 require a declared type (location, dataSync, mediaPlayback…), and some types require extra runtime checks. Starting an FGS from the background is banned since Android 12 (with exemptions: high-priority FCM, exact alarms, user interaction).
